properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB (OU-2) ST10 E-2
properties.Problem_Description:
BACKGROUND
ST10 (DEC file 107.38.064/Hazard ID 336) and ST14 (DEC file 107.38.065/Hazard 340) are managed together.  ST10 includes Spruce Lake and the E-2 POL storage area.  SS14 includes the refueling area located east of the railroad tracks.  ST10 and SS14 are located along Quarry Road in the SE part of the base.  Combined area is approximately 10 acres.  Groundwater is 4-7 feet below ground surface.  The general groundwater gradient is NW.  Groundwater from SS14 flows NW and then N into the lake.

RELEASES
The E-2 POL storage area contained six 672,000 gallon ASTs that stored JP-4, JP-8 and leaded fuels.  There was a significant spill (quantity unknown) within the diked area surrounding AST 6236 in 1967 and a 1,400 gallon spill at Building 6231 in 1999.  A sheen was observed on the surface of Spruce Lake (formerly known as Hardfill Lake) from at least 1978 until 1982.  Suspected releases at SS14 include leaks from fuel lines and spills during unloading and refueling operations.

REMEDIATION
A bioventing system was constructed at ST10/SS14 during the 1995 field season.  In 1996 a soil vapor extraction (SVE) system was installed around Building 6225 due to hydrocarbon vapors inside the building that likely were a result of bioventing.  The ASTs were replaced with a 4,200,000-gallon AST in 2002.  The bioventing system was redesigned and expanded in 2004.  The ST10/SS14 bioventing system and SVE system at Building 6225 ceased operation in 2008.

MOST RECENT ACTIONS
The most recent groundwater monitoring in 2007 detected benzene concentrations up to 67 ug/L.  Additional site characterization is scheduled for 2011.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB (SER-2) (DP55) Birch Lakes
properties.Problem_Description:
Update May 2019- The Air Force soil sampling during an remedial investigation has identified several metals exceeding method two cleanup levels.  In addition, Perfluorooctanoic Acid has been detected above the EPA Lifetime Health Advisory (LHA) of 70 parts per trillion (ppt) in a drinking water well at the Birch Lake Recreational Facilities. The drinking water has been tested in spring and fall since 2016 and levels have been consistently above the LHA with approximately 160 ppt in the spring and as high as 330 ppt in the fall.


Source Area DP55 is a refuse pile directly adjacent to the maintenance yard at the U.S. Air Force recreation site, Birch Lake.  The pile was used to dispose of material associated with the maintenance and operation of the recreation area.  Based on available groundwater data, site visits, and interviews, no contamination exists at DP-55 that poses a risk to human health or the environment (August 1998 RA Report).  Closed.  Reference documents:  Source Evaluation Report 1991 (CH2M), OU-3,4,5 Record of Decision, and 1998 OU-3, 4 and 5 Remedial Action Summary Report.  Last staff assigned were Short, Markey and Farris (rpltr4).

Ponds provide additional contact time for chlorination of primary treated effluent; also serve as diversion ponds for POL spills; major spill of unknown industrial chemical or solvent reported 1975.  Active since 1970.  Currently inactive.  Associated files - 107.07.007, 107.15.004, 107.38.061.  

Includes spill no. 17309932403.  Spill date = 11/20/17; substance = water + 3/% aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) concentrate; quantity = ~100 gallons; description: The bay door  at building 1337 was left open and the pipes froze. properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB (OU-5) LF003
properties.Problem_Description:
LF003 was an active landfill from 1967 - 1987, and it received all base refuse (including household garbage, waste oils, spent solvents, paint residues and thinners, radioactive photographic chemicals and industrial waste). During landfill operations waste was covered with fly ash from the Base power plant. The site was utilized as a fire training area from 1955 to 1989. From 1992 to present day, LF003 has been used as a landfarm to store, segregate, and treat contaminted soil generated from construction operations; to store clean soil, debris, and digested sludge from the water treatment plant; and as a construction laydown yard. 

In 1995, LF003 was assigned active remediation under the 1995 OUs 3, 4, and 5 ROD, and the landfill cover was improved by adding a layer of fly ash and soil. From 1996 - 1998, PCB impacted soil was buried in the southeast of LF003; and additionally a 4.9 acres recycled asphalt pavement cap was installed at the southeast end of the landfill for use as a pad for future landfarming efforts, and 2 feet of additional soil cover was placed in the southeast corner of the landfill to cover exposed debris. 

Annual groundwater monitoring began in 2012, and an RI was completed from 2015 - 2017 to better delineate the extent of contamination. Currently (2025) a supplemental RI is being performed to address data gaps related to incomplete characterization of site contaminants. 

Site also includes spill no. 13309922101; spill date = 8/9/13; substance = investigation-derived waste; quantity = 30 cubic yards of soil spread at cell 1 of landfill 003; PERP file no. 107.02.004.

properties.Site_Name: USCG Port Clarence Loran Station
properties.Problem_Description:
The former Port Clarence LORAN-C Station is located approximately 85 miles northwest of Nome and 75 miles south of the Arctic Circle. The station is situated on Point Spencer, a narrow spit of land extending approximately 15 miles from the Seward Peninsula and enclosing Port Clarence Bay. The area was historically used by indigenous peoples, as evidenced by numerous middens, house remains, and a burial ground located on the spit. Port Clarence is one of the few deep, sheltered harbors on the western coast of Alaska and was historically used by the whaling industry and other sailing vessels, beginning in the 1850s.

In 1925, the United States Coast Guard (USCG) began operating the Point Spencer Light Beacon. The site was most active during the World War II era, during which time the U.S. Army constructed and operated the Port Clarence Army Base (PCAB). PCAB maintained an operational airfield and was left mostly intact when the Army departed in 1955. In 1961, the USCG established the Port Clarence LORAN-C Station, part of a larger system that provide radio navigation aids to the contiguous United States and Alaska. 

In 2010, the LORAN-C signal was terminated for North American, Canadian, and Russian stations. That same year, the 1,350 ft. LORAN tower was demolished, and the remaining station buildings were closed. The former Port Clarence LORAN C Station consists of seven (7) tracts, which include 14 areas of concern (AOCs) where contamination has been found or suspected.

On July 30, 2020, ownership of Tracts 2 and 5 was transferred to Bering Straits Native Corporation.

properties.Site_Name: Fort Wainwright (OU-4) FTWW 038 Landfill Plume
properties.Problem_Description:
The Fort Wainwright Landfill is located at the base of Birch Hill and is 60 acres (approximately 40 acres north of River Road, and approximately 20 acres immediately south of River Road). Landfill activities at this area began in the early 1950s, and waste was initially dumped into gravel pits, burned, and covered. By the early 1960s, trenching and burning of waste ceased and wastes were spread, compacted by a bulldozer, and covered with coal ash generated from the Fort Wainwright power plant. The Operable Unit 4 (OU4) Record of Decision (ROD) remedy included capping the inactive portion of the landfill (this was completed in 1997) and implementing monitored natural attenuation, groundwater monitoring and institutional controls (ICs) to the site. Currently there is a monitoring well network located downgradient (west and southwest) of the capped area. The site is underlain by discontinuous permafrost. Monitoring wells across the site have been installed at shallow (wells screened across the water table), intermediate (wells screened below the water table) and deep (wells screened below permafrost) depths. On an annual basis, ten of the monitoring wells are sampled in the summer, and 7 monitoring wells in the fall. Additionally, an institutional control (IC) inspection is completed annually. Currently, the inactive portion of the landfill is appropriately covered and graded to prevent possible ponding, there is vegetation growth and there have been no signs of damage to the landfill face or slopes. Contaminants of concern remaining above ADEC cleanup levels in the groundwater table are: 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane, 1,1,2-trichloroethane, trichloroethene, benzene and cis-1,2-dichloroethene. Long-term monitoring is expected to continue at this site. The active portion of the landfill is permitted by the Solid Waste Program and monitoring activities are conducted separately under 18 AAC 60. 

The corresponding Army HQAES site number is: 02871.1023.

properties.Site_Name: Fort Wainwright (OU-1) Drum Site West of DRMO FTWW-114
properties.Problem_Description:
The Drums Site West of the Defense Reutilization Marketing Office (DRMO) is approximately 75 acres in size and located west of the DRMO salvage yard on the eastern side of the main cantonment of Fort Wainwright. Several operations and activities have occurred in this area, including a motor pool and automotive maintenance shop in the 1950’s, and a landfill for disposal of solid waste such as porcelain products, refrigerators, ranges, and signposts in the 1960’s and 1970’s. These potential sources were investigated in 1995 as part of Operable Unit 1 (OU1). During training exercises and underground pipeline removal activities in 2013, drums and possible military munitions were encountered. During a visual survey conducted in 2015, ten single drums, two drum piles, several scrap metal piles containing drums and an area of buried drums were identified. A trench (approximately 5 feet wide by 40 feet long) with water was visible. There were no munitions found. Surface soil samples near several partially buried drums, and surface water samples were collected from the trench as part of the 2015 field activities. Diesel range organics (DRO) and residual range organics (RRO) were identified in the surface water above screening levels. All analytes for total aqueous hydrocarbon (TAqH) calculations were not detected, however the limits of detections exceeded screening levels which resulted in TAqH being above the Alaska Water Quality Standard of 0.15 milligrams per liter (mg/L). Arsenic, cadmium, and lead were observed above screening levels however, all results were below the established background levels for the site. Additional investigation of this site is recommended to determine the extent of the drum debris and determine the source of the petroleum contamination in the surface water. During the 2020 per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) preliminary assessment/site investigation, PFOS and PFOA were detected at levels below the screening criteria in well FTWW-AP-5966. Additional work to delineate the PFAS groundwater plume is recommended.

The corresponding Army HQAES site number is: 02871.1111.

properties.Site_Name: JBER-Elmendorf PL081 N. Jet Pipeline
properties.Problem_Description:
North Jet pipline at the western edge of the Base. The site is limited to the abandoned 10 inch pipeline transmitting AVGAS and Jet Fuel Grade 4 (JP-4) that is eligible for DSMOA funding and cleanup and NOT related to the active 12 inch pipeline which is compliance program funded and the one that was found to be leaking in 1994 (associated with spill #s: 94-211238-2 (oil in sewer), 94-211-212- (oil in storm drain)1 and 94-211-257-3 (EAFB pipeline leak) and ledger code LC14999999).  UST Facility ID 1525.  The State Elmendorf Environmental Restoration agreement was abolished on 10/21/2002.  NW1/4 Section 7 PL81 is a fuel pipeline corridor. 

A 10-inch pipeline was constructed in 1942 to transmit AVGAS and JP-4 from the Port of Anchorage to Elmendorf AFB. That pipeline, which was extensively damaged in the 1964 earthquake, was abandoned in place shortly after the earthquake and subsequently removed in 1998. PL81 is in Zone 1 of 3 zones established to better manage sites on the Base. Zone 1 consists of nine plumes located within eight sites.  These sites are spread throughout the northern reaches of Elmendorf AFB (DP98, ST36, ST41, ST61, ST69, LF04, PL81, WP14. With the exception of the DP98 Plume, fuel constituents are the COCs at the Zone 1 plumes.  Chlorinated solvents are the COCs at the DP98 Plume.


The Global Positioning System (GPS) coordinates are 6793997.20 meters north and 345901.25 meters east. 

The 10 inch pipeline unrelated to active 12 inch pipeline that leaked in 1994 down at Port of Anchorage. 

Remedial investigation studies for OU6, which includes the PL81 area, revealed petroleum, oil, and lubricants (POL) contamination from this pipeline. Two plumes (OU6MW-46 and PL81 South) comprise Site PL81. Although this site was not formally identified as a site until after the OU6 ROD was signed, the PL81 area is within the groundwater contamination area addressed by the OU6 ROD. In addition, the two plumes at Site PL81 have the potential to commingle with LF04 groundwater, which is addressed in the OU6 ROD; therefore, groundwater at Site PL81 is addressed under the OU6 ROD. Administratively closed out.

The groundwater zones were established in areas with similar hydrological, geological, geographical, and contamination characteristics, and contain numerous Installation Restoration Program (IRP) sites within each zone.

Potential contaminant sources identified in the vicinity are the Refueler Shop (former Building 149), several former USTs, and a former dry well.  

Groundwater Zone 2 Final Record of Decision was signed by ADEC in December 2002.  The final remedy is Monitored Natural Attenuation, if long-term monitoring does not indicate that cleanup levels will be met within 25 years, or if actions levels are exceeded, then the need to implement an active remediation technique will be evaluated.  The remedy includes: Institutional controls to restrict installation of drinking water wells within the A-Aquifer or other intrusive activities that would not be appropriate during remediation; annual groundwater and surface water monitoring with a five-year review; and groundwater monitoring every 5 years (2007, 2012, 2017, 2022).

properties.Site_Name: King Salmon AS GWZ 5 FT004 Fire Training Area 4
properties.Problem_Description:
Site is within Groundwater Zone 5 (OT31).
Fire Training Area No. 4, potential material disposed includes JP-4 and waste oil/solvents. Perfluorinated compounds (PFC) have been detected in sampling conducted by the Air Force.  This site is located approximately 1600 feet northeast of the centerline of Runway 11/29.  It was used for several years until 1980 for training in fighting aircraft fires.  Old cars were used to simulate aircraft.  Soil and groundwater are contaminated with petroleum and solvents (primarily TCE). 

The following investigation summary was taken from the Final 2014 Remedial Action Construction work plan.  
Surface and Subsurface Soil
Soil samples were collected from FT004 in 1993 and 1996. 

In 1993 (USAF, 1995), three soil borings were drilled at FT004 and one of the borings was completed as a monitoring well. Two to three samples were collected from each boring at five-foot intervals for a total of eight samples (FT04A, B, and C). The samples were analyzed for diesel range organics (DRO), total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPH), volatile organic compounds (VOCs), semi-volatile organic compounds (SVOCs), pesticides, and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs). An additional surface sample was collected and analyzed for dioxins (FT04D). The VOC trichloroethene (TCE) was detected above the ADEC soil cleanup level in one sample (FT04B) at 10 feet below ground surface (bgs). Benzene was detected above the ADEC soil cleanup level in one sample (FT04A), also at 10 feet bgs. In addition, DRO was detected above the soil cleanup level in each borehole. The dioxin 2,3,7,8-Tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD) was detected in one sample at 5.69 pg/g, below the 58 pg/g ADEC Method Two Migration to Groundwater cleanup level (ADEC, 2012).

In 1996 (USAF, 1997), seven subsurface samples were collected from six borings. In addition, five surface samples were collected. DRO was detected above soil cleanup levels in two surface samples and one subsurface (10-feet bgs) sample. TCE was detected in the same samples; however, no TCE detections exceeded the ADEC soil cleanup level.

In May of 2009, Paug-Vik conducted pre-excavation sampling to determine presence or absence of VOCs and dioxins. Four samples were collected at FT004. The VOC 1,3,5- Trimethylbenzene was detected in one sample at 26.6 mg/kg (33.5 mg/kg in the duplicate), above the 23 mg/kg ADEC Method Two Migration to Groundwater cleanup level. Dioxin levels were 1 pg/g or less in each sample. Since no dioxin has been found above cleanup levels in any sample collected in 1996 and in 2009, dioxin is no longer considered a contaminant of concern at this site. In fall 2009, an estimated 1,200 cubic yards of POL-contaminated soil were removed from Site FT004 (PVS, 2010). After the soil was excavated, samples were collected from the excavation walls (the bottom of the excavation reached the water table). Analysis of the samples, which varied in depth from 3 to 10 ft. bgs, indicated soil with various POL concentrations above the cleanup levels was still present at the site. Since TCE was not detected in any 8 of the samples, it is no longer considered a contaminant of concern at this site. The excavation was lined with reinforced plastic sheeting and backfilled with uncontaminated soil. 

In 2011, another 500 cubic yards of POL-contaminated soil were excavated from approximately half the circumference of the original excavation. All confirmation sample results from the 2011 excavation were below cleanup levels for all analytes. The contract limit was reached before the entire circumference could be assessed; soil with POL concentrations above the cleanup levels remains present in the remainder of the 2009 excavation boundary that was not extended in 2011. 

Groundwater
A monitoring well was installed in 1993, and four additional wells were installed in 1996. In May 1997, all five wells (FT04-MW1 through MW5) were sampled (USAF, 2008b). Groundwater samples were analyzed for VOCs, DRO, and gasoline range organics (GRO). Well FT04-MW2 was found to have DRO, TCE, benzene, toluene, and ethylene dibromide (EDB) concentrations above their respective ADEC groundwater cleanup levels. In addition, well FT04-MW4 was found to have a concentration of EDB in exceedance of the ADEC ground water cleanup level. during the 2006 RPO activities (USAF, 2007), one new monitoring well was installed at a location downgradient from the contaminant plume (FT04-MW6). All six wells were sampled at this time; FT04-MW5 had concentrations of TCE, benzene, and toluene above the ADEC groundwater cleanup levels. No VOCs were detected in FT04-MW6, suggesting that this well is located downgradient of the plume. During the 2009 activities, the area around and including FT04-MW5 was excavated

AF point of contact:  Charley Peyton, Project Manager, 611th CES/CEV 10471 20th Street Suite 338, Elmendorf AFB, AK 99506-2270; Telephone 907-552-9765.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB (SS079) Bldg 2207 Dining Hall CITS
properties.Problem_Description:
Former Building 2207/Dining Hall/447 North Street is one of five CITS sites.  There is a municipal drinking water well less than 1 mile upgradient of the site and Garrison Slough is less than 0.25 miles cross-gradient from the site.  95 cubic yards of soil were removed and thermally treated in 2001.

2002 and 2004 soil and groundwater sampling identified DRO above cleanup levels.  The highest DRO concentrations were 23,700 mg/kg and 1.99 mg/L in soil and groundwater, respectively.

In 2006 ADEC requested consideration of possible remedial actions for this site and noted that the site characterization does not adequately characterize the extent of groundwater contamination (a few additional monitoring wells downgradient of the source with confirmation of the local groundwater flow direction are needed).

For your information, (remotely) possible related site.  EiAFB ST59 - Dining Hall; Section 11, T3S, R3E, FM; CSRP Database Reckey 198731X108341, Status: Closed.  CSRP File # 107.38.001.  Diesel spill; contaminated soil has been removed as per Army Memo of 10-20-91.  See also CSRP file# 100.02.003.

The 2019 DD estimated that approximately 2,574 cy of POL-contaminated vadose-zone soil
remained at the site and that the POL impacted groundwater plume extended 171 feet from
north to south, and 108 feet east to west to the southeast of Facility 2207.

The Selected Remedy for the site in the 2019 DD consisted of a remedial excavation of the
impacted vadose zone soil along with MNA of the residual contamination in the groundwater.
The remedial excavation scope planned for the removal of all contaminated vadose zone soil
to the extent practicable as limited by existing in-place infrastructure (i.e., buildings, utilities, roadways, etc.). The MNA scope prescribed the subsequent installation of five groundwater monitoring wells within the plume extents and in areas cross-and down-gradient of the plume boundaries for the purposes of tracking the contaminants migration. The groundwater  monitoring component of the remedy consisted of annual sampling of the groundwater for CoC and MNA concentrations to evaluate the attenuation progress at the site and the
effectiveness of the remedy.

Land Use Controls, including dig and use restrictions, were also implemented for the site until
subsequent monitoring results indicate that the site is eligible for UU/UE. The USAF and
ADEC will perform periodic reviews of the site to assess the remedy progress and ability of
the LUC measures in remaining sufficiently protective of human health and the environment.

The 2019 DD estimated that approximately 2,600 cy of POL contaminated vadose zone soil
remained at the site. The 2022 RA-C remedial excavation removed approximately 1,227 cy of
contaminated soil from the three site excavations. However, due to the proximity of existing
infrastructure and buried utility lines, the excavations were unable to remove the full extent of
contaminated soil. In areas where excavating was restricted, the remnant POL contaminated soil that could be excavated, were it not for infrastructure impingement, extends from beneath an approximately three-foot layer of gravel fill to the depth of groundwater at approximately 8 feet bgs in the vadose zone. The extent of the POL contaminant plume is approximated based on the observed POL contaminant impact in the saturated zone soil in Excavations #1 and #2 and the detected DRO contamination at MW2. Additionally, the analytical data evidences the presence of extensive PFAS contamination in the groundwater throughout the site, specifically PFOS.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB (SS519) Bldg 3426 Supply Facility CITS
properties.Problem_Description:
The second highest DRO reading of at 7,700 mg/kg in soil from the CIT trenches was detected along the western end of Building 3426.  Approximately 25 cubic yards of soil were removed from the location and thermally treated in May 2001.  Further characterization of the site is warranted as only soils pertaining to the CITS Construction Project were removed or tested.

Update: 
Investigations were conducted between 2002 and 2021. Several soil borings and temporary well
points were advanced in the area around the site to define the extent of the affected soil and
groundwater. The results of those investigation efforts identified petroleum contaminated soil in
three distinct areas: Area 1, Area 2, and Area 3. Area 4, located west of the building, does not
include POL-related COCs. POL-contaminated soil at Area 1, located southwest of the
southwestern corner of the building, covers approximately 1,500 square feet. POL-contaminated
soil at Area 2, located south of the southwestern corner of the building and east of Area 1,
covers approximately 2,000 square feet. POL-contaminated soil at Area 3, located south of the
building and east of Area 2, covers approximately 600 square feet. The Decision Document
(USAF 2023a) estimated that 1,200 to 1,500 cubic yards of POL-contaminated soil remained in
these three areas. The Decision Document (USAF 2023a) showed the POL groundwater
contamination plume on the west side of the building beginning at the approximate middle of the
building and extending south approximately 100 feet past the building corner. The plume was
estimated to be approximately 275 feet long by 100 feet wide. Contaminated soil was identified
above and below the groundwater table.

This site is within the known perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) groundwater plume beneath the central portion of Eielson AFB. 

In 2024 Remedial Action was conducted on three excavations at this site and in that report, the conceptual model for the site is recommended to be updated as follows: The soil and groundwater COCs for Site SS519 are POL-related compounds GRO, DRO, 1,3,5-
trimethylbenzene, 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene, ethylbenzene, xylenes, 1,4-dichlorobenzene,
naphthalene, 1- methyl naphthalene, 2-methyl naphthalene and 1,1’ biphenyl in soil; and GRO,
DRO, naphthalene, and 1-methyl naphthalene in groundwater. Non-petroleum-related
contaminants of potential concern (COPCs) for Site SS519 are chloroform, trichloroethylene,
chromium, and thallium in soil; and arsenic, cobalt, iron, and manganese in groundwater.
Exposure media and pathways at Site SS519 are dermal exposure to and ingestion of
contaminated soil (subsurface) and groundwater, and inhalation of outdoor and indoor air.
Current and future receptors for soil, groundwater, and air media include commercial and
industrial workers, construction workers, and site visitors, trespassers, and recreational users.
Future receptors include hypothetical residents. The area is not used for hunting, subsistence,
or farming.

Approximately 1,312 LCY of POL-contaminated soil were excavated from three areas at Site SS519, of which 213 LCY of soil were co-contaminated with PFAS. Lateral extents of the excavation were limited by infrastructure, and vertical extents were limited to minimize removal of PFAS-affected soils in the smear zone. Six permanent groundwater monitoring wells were installed for inclusion in the base groundwater monitoring network. Groundwater monitoring revealed exceedances of POL-related contaminants in two wells and PFAS in one well.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Homer Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: Site characterization activities were conducted in 2021 to evaluate per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) at the Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities (ADOT&PF) Homer Airport (HOM). Potential sources of PFAS at the HOM facility include fire training activities using aqueous film forming foam (AFFF). Fire training activities were likely conducted twice per year since the 1970s at two AFFF training areas and at least once per year at various locations along the airport runways.  There are no known emergency response incidents where AFFF use was documented.  The precise timeline and locations of AFFF use are unknown.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Cold Bay Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: In April 2022, Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (ADEC) collected water samples from potable wells in the immediate vicinity of the Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities (ADOT&PF) Cold Bay Airport. Analytical sample results indicated concentrations of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) above 70 ppt in both municipal wells located at the Cold Bay Water Treatment Plant. In November 2022, a water supply well search for wells not connected to the municipal water system was conducted. The results of the water supply well search revealed that Well #2, which was formerly below the ADEC Action Level, now exceeded the level. Samples results from Well #3 and throughout various other points in the water supply system contained one or more PFAS constituents above ADEC Action Levels. Six private water supply wells were sampled, one contained PFAS and PFOA constituents above the DEC Action Level.

properties.Site_Name: Ketchikan Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: ADOT&PF is conducting a well search and sampling effort to evaluate PFAS impacts in the vicinity of the Ketchikan Airport.

properties.Site_Name: ARNG Nome AAOF
properties.Address_1: Army National Guard Nome Army Aviation Operating Facility
properties.Problem_Description: Five 5-gallon buckets of Chemguard 3% AFFF concentrate and a single Tri-Max fire extinguisher were discovered at the ARNG Nome AAOF during a preliminary assessment. No records of the maintenance or use of the Tri-Max extinguisher were found. The AAOF is not equipped with a AFFF fire suppression system. After a Site Inspection in September 2021 in which 6 soil borings (18 primary soil samples) were advanced and completed as monitoring wells (6 primary groundwater samples), multiple PFAS compounds were detected in soil and groundwater. Only PFOS exceeded current DEC cleanup levels in soil, and there were no exceedances in groundwater above current DEC cleanup levels.

properties.Site_Name: Eareckson Air Station SS23
properties.Problem_Description:
Eareckson AS is situated on Shemya Island, approximately 1,500 miles southwest of Anchorage, Alaska at the westernmost tip of the Aleutian Islands.  Shemya Island is part of the Near Islands group of the Aleutian Archipelago. The U.S. Army first developed facilities on Shemya Island in 1943 to support operations against the Japanese occupation forces on the nearby islands of Attu, Agattu, and Kiska. In 1954, the site was deactivated, and was turned over to the Civil Aeronautics Authority in 1955. In 1958, the Air Force returned to Shemya Island to support various Air Force and Army strategic intelligence gathering activities. It has remained active in this capacity to the present. In 1995, the station was downsized and reverted to caretaker status and a private operation and maintenance contractor took control of the facility under contract to the Air Force. Shemya Island is owned by the U.S. Government and is under the jurisdiction of the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) as part of the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge. 


SS023 consists of seven asphalt-covered hardstands, one previously existing asphalt hardstand(now removed), and the areas between them. The hardstands are located on the southeast side of the old Abandoned Runway C on the western portion of Shemya Island.  These hardstands were originally constructed to park fighter aircraft during WWII. During the 1980s, some of these hardstands were used for drum cleaning and crushing operations, as well as drum storage. Before the 1980s, at least three of the hardstands contained numerous drums. POLs, petroleum wastes, and solvents were potentially disposed at this site.

properties.Site_Name: Eareckson Air Station FT02
properties.Problem_Description:
Eareckson AS is situated on Shemya Island, approximately 1,500 miles southwest of Anchorage, Alaska at the westernmost tip of the Aleutian Islands.  Shemya Island is part of the Near Islands group of the Aleutian Archipelago. Shemya Island is owned by the U.S. Government and is under the jurisdiction of the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) as part of the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge. The U.S. Army first developed facilities on Shemya Island in 1943 to support operations against the Japanese occupation forces on the nearby islands of Attu, Agattu, and Kiska. In 1954, the site was deactivated, and was turned over to the Civil Aeronautics Authority in 1955. In 1958, the Air Force returned to Shemya Island to support various Air Force and Army strategic intelligence gathering activities. It has remained active in this capacity to the present. In 1995, the station was downsized and reverted to caretaker status and a private operation and maintenance contractor took control of the facility under contract to the Air Force.

FT002 is located on the western end of the island and consists of three areas: Aircraft Mock-Up Area(MA), Fire Training Area (FTA), and Abandoned Drum Disposal Area (ADDA).  The MA was used for fire-fighting training from 1983 to 1988. Cylindrical tanks were configured to resemble an aircraft fuselage, which were located within two concentric earthen berms on asphalt. Petroleum products were used as accelerants during fire training at the site. From 1996 through 2000, a bioventing system was installed and operated to remediate petroleum contamination. The FTA was used for fire training activities from the early 1970s to the mid-1980s. Debris and approximately 1,100 cubic yards of petroleum contaminated soils were removed to a depth of 3 to 4 feet in the late 1980s.  The ADDA is a drainage on the north side of the abandoned runway that was used to dispose of drums. Approximately 30 buried drums and 35 to 40 cubic yards of visibly contaminated sediments were removed in 1996.  

Petroleum and PFAS contamination is present at this site.  Institutional controls are effectively controlling human exposure to contamination.  The risk of contamination to ecological receptors is currently unknown.

properties.Site_Name: Eareckson Air Station OT48
properties.Problem_Description: Site OT048 is the Water Gallery and collection point of potable water used at Eareckson Air Station located on the north side of the airfield on Shemya Island, Alaska. Water reaches OT048 by drainage from a series of shallow ponds located to the north. Water flowing through OT048 eventually drains into Gallery Creek which is the only significant surface-water body near OT048. Potable water is collected and treated by an on-site infiltration system which has received multiple upgrades over the years (the system has been in operation since the 1950s). Fuel and/or solvent spill areas and potential contaminant source areas from base activities are located within the drainage basin supporting the Water Gallery. Environmental site investigations began in 1992. Petroleum contaminated soils were identified and removed in 1989. The excavated areas were backfilled with clean sand. Surface water, sediment and groundwater were sampled, and trichloroethene (TCE) was detected at concentrations above the Table C cleanup levels. TCE will be monitored every two years at the site until the concentration falls below the Table C cleanup levels for two consecutive sampling events. Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) were first identified at this site in 2018. A remedial investigation (RI) was conducted in 2021 and 2023 to determine the nature and extent of PFAS contamination. Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic Acid (PFOS) were detected in the soil, and PFOA and PFOS were detected in the groundwater above project screening levels. The PFAS plume in this area extends from Hangar 3 and 4 (upgradient from the site) to south of OT048 and to the Pacific Ocean. The nature and extent of the PFAS plume was sufficiently characterized during the RI effort, and no additional investigation of PFAS is planned for this site. Water from the Water Gallery for drinking water continues to be treated and sampled regularly. Long-term monitoring and institutional control inspections continue for this site.

properties.Site_Name: Indian Mt. LRRS (All Sites)
properties.Problem_Description: Site operated 1951 to present.  Over 60,000 gallons of fuel spilled at upper/lower camps in late 1970s and early 1980s.  Known contaminants include petroleum products, halogenated/non-halogenated solvents, and PCBs.  The White Alice site was deactivated in 1979.  Aircraft Control and Warning site was deactivated in 1984.  1987 demolition of some W/A and AC&W facilities in 1987.  The installation is currently an Active Long Range Radar Station operated by the US Air Force. Cleanup is being conducted under the DoD Installation Restoration Program (IRP).  Individual IRP sites in the CS database include: LF004, LF005, LF006, OT008, SD001, SD007, SS002, SS003, SS009, and SS010. Please see these individual sites for more detailed description of the investigation and remediation activities that have occurred.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB (OU-1) (ST020) Refueling Loop
properties.Problem_Description:
Aircraft refueling loop with three complexes: E-7, E-8 and E-9.  Each complex includes an asphalt pad with adjacent areas of gravel and grass.  Each complex has its own pump house (E-7: Bldg 1315, E-8: Bldg 1321, E-9: Bldg 1305), three 50,000-gallon USTs, one 25,000-gallon defueling UST and underground fueling and defueling lines.

Groundwater is approximately 3-9 feet below ground surface.  The large area enclosed by the taxiway loop north of E-7 contains surface water ponds.  Garrison Slough is approximately 1,000 feet from E-7.

Contamination is thought to be due to a variety of spills and leaks.  Floating product up to 30-cm thick was measured above shallow groundwater at each of the three complexes.
E-7: JP-4 leaks in subsurface fueling and defueling transfer pipes
E-8: JP-4 surface spills from overfilling storage tanks
E-9: (1) "extensive" leak detected Aug 1988, repairs Jun 1989, amount unknown; (2) leak on tarmac detected and repaired Jun 1989, amount unknown; (3) Leak in line to defueling tank detected Jun 1992, repaired Jul 1992, amount unknown.

Bioventing systems at E-7 and E-9 were used from 1991-2002.  E-7 and E-8 were last monitored in 2002.  Benzene at E-7 remains at concentrations up to 82.9 ug/L in groundwater.  E-8 has benzene up to 46 ug/L.  E-9 was most recently monitored in 2007.  Several monitoring wells at E-7 and E-9 have shown fluctuations.

2011 field work will include further soil and groundwater site characterization.

The Type III Hydrant Refueling System is a large compliance restoration site (DEC file 107.38.106/Hazard ID 4394) that encompasses ST20. 

This site also includes spill no. 17309906903; spill date = 3/10/17; substance = unknown; quantity = unknown; source = unknown; location = parking lot west of bldg. 1306, 64.650771, -147.056538, WGS84; PPRP file no. 107.02.004. Description: contamination discovered via field screening during geotechnical work (PID 50ppm in soil at 2.5 feet bgs).  Soil cuttings were placed in drum #9129 and stored at LF003 pending analysis. 

This site also includes spill no. 23309924201; spill date = 8/30/2023; Transfer line 3 sustained a leak when a gasket broke during transfer 30AUG23; Estimated 500 gallons of JP-8 spilled; Free flowing fuel recovered with vacuum trailer; Absorbent boom placed to prevent adjacent pond from being impacted. COCs are similar to ST020. 

This site also includes spill no. 22309932102: EAFB Pipeline JP-8 > 500 gal. Transferred from PPR to CS on 8/20/2025. PPR number 23309924201. Spill date = 8/30/2023. Spill of Aviation Fuel; estimated 500 gallons.


This site also includes spill no. 23309931301: EAFB Building 1308 JP-8 Seal Failure, spill date = 11/9/2023; estimated 839 gallons JP-8.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB (OU-7)(SS067) Garrison Slough PCBs
properties.Problem_Description:
Garrison Slough begins in a marshy area at the south end of Eielson AFB and flows north-northwest through the developed portion of the base.  It consists primarily of engineered drainage channels 10 to 50 feet wide.  The water surface is approximately 8 to 10 feet below surrounding grade and the water in the slough is approximately 2 to 4 feet deep.  Garrison Slough drains into Moose Creek, which flows into Piledriver Slough, which flows into the Tanana River approximately 2 miles northwest of base.

PCB contamination is thought to originate from past releases to surface soil at the unpaved drainage channel located approximately 900 feet upstream of the Arctic Avenue/Manchu Road bridge.  PCBs have been found in soil, sediment and fish tissue.  The contaminated site is defined as the part of Garrison Slough originating approximately 1,000 feet upstream of Arctic Avenue and extending downstream to the confluence of Moose Creek and Garrison Slough.  The site also includes a portion of the bank adjacent to the source area.  The main exposure pathway is contaminant transfer to fish through sediment and then to humans.

Current institutional controls at this site include fishing restrictions (catch-and-release only) and fish control gates near the downstream edge of base.  Contaminated sediments were excavated in 1996-7.  Sediments from one portion of the site were not excavated due to discovery of an unexploded ordnance.

PCB (Aroclor 1260) concentrations in fish tissue ranged from 240 to 310 ug/kg in 2007.  Off-base samples ranged from 10 to 150 ug/kg.  PCBs (Aroclor 1260) in sediment were as high as 16,000 ug/L.  A comprehensive fish tissue and sediment study will be conducted in 2011 or 2012.  

The AF conducted a Supplemental Remedial Investigation (SRI) in 2012/2013.  Soil, sediment and fish tissue were sampled and analyzed for PCBs, pesticides and mercury.  In general, soil and sediment PCB concentrations were below 5 ppm with the exception of two hot spots in the western region of the ditch. Pesticide concentrations were well below the soil cleanup levels, but exceeded the more stringent sediment screening levels. Hg only exceeded the action limit of 0.07 ppm in one sediment sample. Samples from the previously dreged areas of the slough detected lower concentrations of contaminants, and did not appear to be "recontaminating" due to movement of sediments in the slough. Fish tissue concentrations continue to decline, though were still significantly higher in Fish from Garrison Slough than in fish from other water bodies.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB (OU-7) (SER-1) (SS062) Garrison Slough
properties.Problem_Description:
PCB contamination was found in sediment and soil in Garrison Slough.  Pesticides have been detected in the soil.  Possibly contaminated groundwater and surface runoff from site.  Garrison Slough is primary SW drainage through base.  Garrison Slough is a main drainage ditch at Eielson.  The site is defined as that portion of Garrison Slough originating approximately 1,000 feet upstream of Arctic Avenue and extending downstream tot he confluence of Moose Creek and Garrison Slough.  The site also includes a portion of the bank adjacent to the origin of the source.  The main exposure pathway is contaminant transfer to fish through sediment and then to humans.  The site is assigned a HIGH overall risk on the Air Force Relative Risk Evaluation Worksheet dated 10/25/95.

Coordinates for site are located at Reach 1A.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB (OU-4) (SS035) Asphalt Mix Area
properties.Problem_Description:
Mixing area for asphalt and base for road oiling operation; commingled waste oils and solvents mixed with contaminated fuels; possible disposal of 200 empty asphalt drums at site.  DDT was found in the soil and sediments, not in the groundwater.  Active Early 1950s to late 1960s.  Currently inactive.  The site is assigned a HIGH overall risk on the Air Force Relative Risk Evaluation Worksheet dated 12/4/95.    (rpltr4)

2020 Update
The SS035 Asphalt Mix Area site contains the Garrison Slough Pond.  Surface water sampling conducted during the 2018-2019 remedial investigation identified Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS)and Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) at concentrations greater than the DEC Table C groundwater cleanup levels.  Five other perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) were also detected.

properties.Site_Name: AIA Fire Training Pit
properties.Problem_Description: Petroleum contaminated soils identified during 1988 site investigation.  Soil contamination restricted to site.  Unknown extent of contamination.  On-site soil remediation began 5/89.  Estimated 7,000 cubic yards to be treated.  On-site treatment consisted of landfarming/surface spreading in 0.5 feet lifts.  Remediation taking longer than anticipated.

properties.Site_Name: Galena AFS/Airport - FT001 Fire Train. Area
properties.Problem_Description:
Last Updated: November 6, 2017

The Fire Protection Training Area (FPTA; Site FT001) is located at the east end of the Former Galena Forward Operating Location (FOL), north of the runway overrun. Soil and groundwater investigations were conducted at the site between 1986 - 2013. Site FT001 is contaminated with multiple petroleum-related compounds, trichloroethene (TCE), perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS). Contamination in soil and groundwater is attributed to the use of up to 28,000 gallons of fuel, annually, for fire training exercises conducted from the late 1950s through 1985. Contamination is also attributed to spills and leaks from drums that may have been stored around the edge of the FPTA circle. Fire extinguishing agents used at Site FT001 included protein foam, chlorobromomethane, dry chemical, halon, and aqueous film forming foam (AFFF).

The Interim Record of Decision (ROD) for Site FT001 addresses cleanup of petroleum compounds and TCE. Proposed remedies include bioventing, soil-vapor extraction (SVE), natural attenuation, and land use controls (LUC) to mitigate potential exposures until Cleanup Complete is achieved. PFOA and PFOS are considered “emerging contaminants,” and the Air Force is managing the evaluation of these compounds under a separate program. As such, the Interim ROD for Site FT001 does not address PFOA and PFOS contamination in soil or groundwater.

As of November 6, 2017, the Interim ROD is pending approval.

properties.Site_Name: NARL - Airstrip Fuel Spill
properties.Problem_Description: The Airstrip Site, also known as Site 5, consists of approximately 150 acres bound by the Chukchi Sea to the north, North Salt Lagoon and U.S. Air Force (USAF) property to the south and east, and Imikpuk Lake to the southwest. The site has a 5,000-foot runway, a large hangar, an apron area, and other buildings, including the Former Naval Arctic Research Laboratory (NARL) Treatment Plant. Several fuel spills occurred on the site between 1976 and 1987. Fuel reportedly released at this site includes gasoline and jet propellant No. 5 (JP-5). In response to these spills, several investigations and remedial actions were completed, including the installation of a fuel recovery trench and a 1,720-foot-long subsurface ice-barrier wall (containment berm/barrier) between 1996 and 2002. In addition, approximately 4,000 feet of underground fuel pipeline connecting the Airstrip Site to the Powerhouse Site was excavated and removed in 1997. A removal action in 2002 removed 2,268 cubic yards of contaminated soil. In 2002, an investigation indicated that the free product remaining at the site exists in isolated pockets within the permafrost and, as a result, is relatively immobile. A Decision Document was produced in 2002. Long-term monitoring over subsequent years has documented DRO below the cleanup level (CLUs)(8,200 ug/L) in active-zone water. GRO remains above CULs. PFAS were detected above CULs in 2021, and a Risk Assessment Work Plan for PFAS Remedial Investigation was completed in Fall 2025. The documents regarding PFAS are in the 310.38.037 NARL Sitewide PFAS file.

properties.Site_Name: JBER-Elmendorf OU3 SD016 Bldg 8197
properties.Problem_Description:
In the 1950s and 1960s, the Air Force disposed of a variety of shop-generated wastes here, including solvents, paint thinners, and other liquid wastes, into open trenches or applied directly on the soil. Due to regrading and revegetation of part of the source area, the exact locations of the former ditch and disposal areas were unknown.  Groundwater contamination for OU3 is divided into two areas-East Groundwater area which covers SD16 and West Groundwater area. Formerly D-17 Shop Wase Disposal Site. 

Currently in Zone 3 groundwater management area consists (as of 2010): LF59, ST37 (Fairchild Avenue, Kenney Avenue, Slammer Avenue, OU3MW-25 Plume, OU5MW-02 Plume, SP1-02 Plume, Seeps, Surface, Water and Wetland Remediation System, Early Warning and Sentry Well Network). Trenches used for waste disposal (SD16) are suspected to be the source of TCE contamination in the Fairchild Avenue Plume; however, the source area(s) has not been confirmed. 

Original OU list: Operable Unit #1 (Million Gallon Hill Area)-Sites SP-5/5A, OT-1, D-15, D-16, D-17, NS-2. 
Operable Unit #2 (Air Force High Priority Sites-Sites S-5, D-4, D-10, FT-1. 
Operable Unit #3 (Landfills)-Sites D-5, D-6, D-7, D-8, D-9, D-11, D-12, D-13, NS-2. Operable Unit #4 (Hangar Floor Drains)-Sites IS-1, IS-2, IS-3, IS-4, IS-5, IS-6, IS-7, IS-8. 
Operable Unit #5 (Fuel Spill Sites)-Sites SP-1 thru SP-16, NS-3. 
Operable Unit #6 (UST/LUST Sites)-Approx. 35 known UST/LUST sites scattered around facility. 
Operable Unit #7 (Misc. Sites)-Sites D-1, D-2, D-3, RD-1, S-l, S-3, S-4, S-6, S-7.

Former file# CS77.15 SD16 OU = operable unit, SD = surface runoffs, wash racks, ditches, oil/water separators.  Site is located east of Building 31-260 south of the west ramp a.k.a. OU 3 East.   SD16 is in Zone 3 of 3 zones established to better manage sites on the Base. Zone 3 consists of 10 plumes spread across the sourthern portion of Elmendorf AFB. 

East groundwater area in OU3 encompassess the area coverd by soils areas of interest: SD16, SS21 and the east intersource area (including the source SD31 excavation). SD16 encompasses three areas: The Solvent Disposal Trench area, the Heavy Equipment Storage area and the Snow Accumulation Area. 

The west groundwater area includes monitoring wells in the vicinity of receptor SD52 and the west intersource area. 

Now referred to as Disaster Preparedness bldg.

EPA ID: AK8570028649

Cherry Hill drainage ditch was an artificial drainage channel which received storm drainage from drains under a runway and possibly from other shop drains on base.  It flowed westward from the East-West runway toward the Kink Arm (Cook Inlet). Halogenated hydrocarbons, solvents, oils, detergents, present. properties.Site_Name: Point Barrow POW-M Dewline Site Vehicle Maintenance Facility Area (SS002)
properties.Address_1: Point Barrow Long Range Radar Station
properties.Problem_Description:
Site operated 1953 to present.  Possible contaminants include unknown quantities of petroleum products, halogenated solvents.  Small area affected by petroleum leak near tank farm.  Extent of contamination otherwise unknown.  Also see 350.45.002.  EPA ID# AK1570028695--CERCLIS site.  DSMOA site. (rpltr8).  Two sites are listed on the Air Force Relative Risk Evaluation Worksheets dated 9/3/95:  a garage (IRP site SS002) and a diesel fuel spill (IRP site SS001).  Both sites are assigned an overall risk of HIGH on the worksheets.  The worksheets identify exposure pathways of inhalation/ingestion of soil/dust and ingestion of surface water for humans; ingestion/inhalation of soil/dust and ingestion of surface water and sediment for other mammals; ingestion of surface water and sediment for birds; and direct contact for aquatic organisms.  Last staff assigned were Cutler and Stephens.

The Vehicle Maintenance Facility (VMH) Area is located within USAF ERP Site SS002.  Four distinct source areas at the main installation are located within SS002: the Vehicle Maintenance Area, the Vehicle Fueling Station Area, the Radome Area, and the Transformer Stand Area.  The VMH is located west of Module Train A.  The building was constructed in 1953 and is still an active vehicle maintenance and storage facility.  This area was investigated in the 1996 Remedial Investigation Report due to concerns about release of liquids to the ground surface from floor drains.  Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) were detected in soil underneath the building at a maximum concentration of 370 mg/kg; DRO was detected up to 7,700 mg/kg.  PCBs were detected in soil at the west end of the building, apparently from washout of soil from underneath the building.  PCBs were also detected in tundra soil on south side of road that parallels the south side of the building.  An interim removal action in 2006 removed PCB contaminated soil to permafrost in a 30 foot square area immediately west of the building.  Confirmation samples showed PCBs remaining in the soil up to 53 mg/kg along the southern portion of the excavation.  The volume of soil with PCBs greater than 1 mg/kg in the areas around the building is estimated at 178 cubic yards. The volume of soil with PCBs greater than 1 mg/kg underneath the building is estimated at 189 cubic yards.

properties.Site_Name: Fort Wainwright (OU-5) EQFS FTWW-094
properties.Problem_Description:
The East Quartermaster Fueling System (EQFS) area covers approximately 40 acres between Taxiway 18 and the Chena River between Building 1579 to the southwest and Building 1054 to the northeast. The EQFS was used for vehicle storage and maintenance, dry cleaning, fuels testing, refueling, pesticide storage mixing, and waste storage. Suspected sources include spills and leaks from pipelines, fueling stations and undocumented spills. The EQFS area included underground storage tanks (USTs), aboveground storage tanks (ASTs), a pump house, and fueling islands which have all been removed. Contaminants of concern at the EQFS are benzene, 1,2-ethylene dibromide, 1,1,1-trichloroethane (1,1,1-TCA) and trichloroethene (TCE) in the groundwater, and petroleum products and xylenes in the soil. To address the petroleum and solvent contamination an air sparge (AS)/soil vapor extraction (SVE) system was installed on the east side of Building 1060 in 1994. The system operated from 1994 to 1999 on the east side of Building 1060 before the system was moved to the west side of Building 1060 in 2000. By 2005, the groundwater remedial action goals had been met, so the system was turned off and decommissioned in 2010. Long-term monitoring activities at the EQFS have been focused on evaluating the residual groundwater contamination in the former Building 1060 treatment area. In 2017 monitoring wells on the east side of Building 1060 were sampled and trichloroethene (TCE) was detected above the remedial action goal of 5 micrograms per liter. Monitoring wells at the Building 1060 area are sampled annually to monitor the TCE and petroleum concentrations. Other areas within EQFS, the remedy in the Record of Decision (ROD) was for natural attenuation. Institutional control inspections are conducted annually. Long-term monitoring efforts are expected to continue at this site.
 
This site also includes spill no. 12309912901; contaminated gravel discovered on 5/8/2012 during a parking lot repaving project at Building 1060.

The corresponding Army HQAES site number is: 02871.1071.

properties.Site_Name: Fort Wainwright (OU-2) FTWW 047 DRMO
properties.Problem_Description:
The Defense Reutilization Marketing Office (DRMO) Yard is a fenced area of approximately 25 acres located in the southeast portion of the U.S. Army Garrison Alaska Fort Wainwright. Historical activities conducted at the DRMO Yard included vehicle maintenance, drum storage, and open burning. The site was operated as a vehicle maintenance shop from 1945 to 1961 when it was converted to a salvage yard. A remedial investigation (RI)/feasibility study (FS) was conducted in 1995, and based on results, the DRMO Yard was divided into five subareas. DRMO1 and DRMO4 are being cleaned up under the Three-Party (and Operable Unit 2 Record of Decision), and DRMO2 (Former Building 5001), DRMO3 and DRMO5 (across Channel B) are being cleaned up under the Two-Party Agreement. DRMO1 and DRMO4 are currently being sampled for diesel range organics (DRO), benzene, tetrachloroethene (PCE), trichloroethene (TCE), cis-1,2-dichlorethene, 1,1-dichloroethene and vinyl chloride on an annual basis (during the fall typically). DRMO2 (former Building 5001) and DRMO5 (across Channel B) are sampled for petroleum (DRO) and natural attenuation parameters. DRMO2 is sampled annually, and DRMO5 is sampled every five years for the Five-Year Review. DRMO3 is not actively being remediated, and there has been no groundwater sampling in this area since 1994. Long-term monitoring of the groundwater continues at the DRMO Yard to monitor groundwater concentrations and plume stability trends. Institutional control inspections are conducted annually.

The corresponding Army HQAES site number is: 02871.1024. This site also includes spill numbers 10309911902 and 10309911903.

properties.Site_Name: Fort Wainwright (OU-4) FTWW 037 FireTrain Area
properties.Problem_Description:
The Fort Wainwright Fire Training Pits (FTP) are located south of Montgomery Road in the southeast corner of the Ladd Army Airfield. The FTP source area consists of FTP 3A, FTP 3B and a depression area. The FTPs were used for the training of fire department and rescue crews at Fort Wainwright. The bottoms of the FTPs were not lined when constructed. Activities included soaking pit soils with water; filling the pit with fuel; igniting the flammable mixture; and extinguishing the resultant fire. It has been estimated that 1,500 to 2,300 gallons of flammable liquids were burned per year in the FTPs. The Operable Unit 4 (OU4) Record of Decision (ROD) found that removal of contaminated soils at the FTPs would adequately protect human health and the environment. A total of 1860 cy of contaminated soil were excavated in 1996. Confirmation soil sampling indicated all petroleum contaminated soil had been removed. Additional investigations were conducted in 2013 due to concerns regarding the potential for the presence of per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) contamination at this site. Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) were both detected above the promulgated ADEC cleanup levels and EPA Lifetime Health Advisory (LHA) of 70 parts per trillion. This site was added to the Army’s PFAS preliminary assessment (PA) /site inspection (SI) as an area of potential interest (AOPI). Additional PFAS samples were collected in 2020, and results are currently in regulatory review. Additional site characterization work is recommended for this site.

The corresponding Army HQAES site number is: 02871.1022.

properties.Site_Name: Fort Greely Former Fire Training Area BRAC 85S
properties.Problem_Description:
This site is generally known as Firefighter Training Area South, and is investigated under the Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) program known as Parcel 85 South (85S). The site consisted of a depression with a rectangular pit in the center of the training area, and a drum storage area on the western edge of the pit. This site is located southeast of the southeast corner of the Allen Army Airfeld (AAAF). Several environmental investigations have occurred over the years at this site. During an initial soil investigation in 1991, benzene, diesel range organics (DRO), bunker C fuel oil,  dichlorodiphenyldichloroethane (DDD), dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) and dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDE) were identified. From 1995 to 1997, in situ bioremediation (land farming) was used to treat surface soil, and bioventing was used to treat subsurface soil. This remediation effort went on for two years. Additional investigations to delineate the contaminated soil after the remediation efforts occurred in 1998, 2005, 2007 and 2008. In 2007, multiple soil borings were drilled to 60 feet below ground surface (bgs), and only gasoline range organics (GRO) was identified in the soil at varied concentrations. From 2003 to 2011, groundwater monitoring wells were installed and sampled. TCE was detected above groundwater cleanup levels in Monitoring Well (MW)-2 from 2003-2007. In 2016 Perfluorooctane Sulfonate (PFOS) and Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) were added to the groundwater monitoring program. PFOS and PFOA have been detected below the project action level of 0.4 µg/L but above the EPA Health Advisory level of 0.07 µg/L. Groundwater monitoring is expected to continue at this site.

The U.S. Army HQAES site number is: 02341.1006. Associated sites; Fort Greely Former Fire Training Area BRAC 133 (Hazard ID: 4246) and Fort Greely Former Fire Training Area BRAC 85N (Hazard ID: 4245).

Transformer oil containing PCB was reportedly burned in a shallow pit in the area now paved as the parking lot south of Building 35-750.  The approximate location of the former burn pit area. Additionally, PCB-contaminated soil may have been spread along the paved access road and parking lot during grading activities prior to paving in 1997. properties.Site_Name: Eareckson Air Station FT03
properties.Problem_Description:
Eareckson AS is situated on Shemya Island, approximately 1,500 miles southwest of Anchorage, Alaska at the westernmost tip of the Aleutian Islands. Shemya Island is part of the Near Islands group of the Aleutian Archipelago. The U.S. Army first developed facilities on Shemya Island in 1943 to support operations against the Japanese occupation forces on the nearby islands of Attu, Agattu, and Kiska. In 1954, the site was deactivated, and was turned over to the Civil Aeronautics Authority in 1955. In 1958, the Air Force returned to Shemya Island to support various Air Force and Army strategic intelligence gathering activities. It has remained active in this capacity to the present. In 1995, the station was downsized and reverted to caretaker status and a private operation and maintenance contractor took control of the facility under contract to the Air Force.  Shemya Island is owned by the U.S. Government and is under the jurisdiction of the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) as part of the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge. 


FT003, the Fire Department Foam Training Area is located in the west central area
of the island.  Materials disposed of include combustibles, JP-4, waste oil, and POLs at site.  Fire training discontinued in late 1980s.  Surface water drainages are within the site boundary.  Groundwater at 40' below ground surface.

properties.Site_Name: Eareckson Air Station ST50
properties.Problem_Description:
Site ST050 is located on the western side of Shemya Island, Alaska as part of the Eareckson Air Station and includes the Alcan Tank Farm. The Alcan Tank Farm originally consisted of seven bulk aboveground storage tanks (ASTs), and one underground storage tank (UST). One AST (Tank 7) and the UST (Tank 5) have been removed. The tanks and pipelines present at this site were constructed in the 1950’s and used to store motor vehicle gas (MOGAS), Jet Propellant (JP)-4, JP-8. Site investigations have been conducted at this site since 1988. From all the site investigation work, diesel range organics (DRO), gasoline range organics (GRO), trichloroethene (TCE), polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH) and other fuel constituents (such as benzene) have been detected at concentrations above cleanup levels in the soil and groundwater. A Record of Decision was finalized and signed in 2014, with the selected remedy for ST050 being long-term management with institutional controls for all media and monitored natural attenuation for groundwater. TCE was the only contaminant detected in the groundwater above cleanup levels in 2021.

In 2021 and 2023 the groundwater and soil were sampled for per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and perfluorohexanesulfonic acid (PFHxS) were detected in the groundwater above the project screening levels (PSLs) around Tank 6 and Tank 8 within the ST050/SS062P site boundary. There were no PFAS detections in the soil.

ST050 has two other sites overlapping: Site CS566 (See DEC File Number: 2649.38.051, Hazard ID: 26300), and SS062P (SS062P is a separate site to track PFAS within the existing ST050, no separate File number or Hazard ID is available for this, site is being tracked under ST050).

properties.Site_Name: Clear SFS Site 06 WP006
properties.Problem_Description: Site 6 is the historic sludge pit associated with the station sewage treatment plant.  The treatment plant is located halfway between the construction camp and the composite area and consists of an Imhoff tank, leach field and the sludge pit.  The sludge pit has now been replaced by a lined drying bed.  Before the costruction of the new lined drying bed, sludge from the Imhoff tank was pumped to the unlined sludge pit and allowed to dewater prior to disposal in the station landfill.  Surface soil sampling at Site 6, Abandoned Sludge Pit, detected maximum levels of  polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) – 183 mg/kg, 4-chloroaniline – 5.7 mg/kg, mercury – 9.9 mg/kg, cadmium – 7.4 mg/kg, lead – 630 mg/kg, selenium – 21 mg/kg, barium – 2600 mg/kg, chromium – 71 mg/kg, silver – 28 mg/kg, and arsenic – 15 mg/kg.

properties.Site_Name: Fort Greely Former Fire Training Area BRAC 85N
properties.Problem_Description:
This site is generally known as Firefighter Training Area North, and is investigated under the Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) program known as Parcel 85 North (85N). This site consisted of a depression with a rectangular pit located near the center. Aerial photographs taken in 1969 showed a drum storage area in the southwestern side of the pit. This site is located north of the east end of the west taxiway of the Allen Army Airfield (AAAF) in the Fort Greely cantonment. During an initial soil investigation in 1991, diesel range organics (DRO), pesticides [dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethanewere (DDT), dichlorodiphenyldichloroethane (DDD) and dichlorodiphenyldichloroethylene (DDE)] trichloroethene (TCE) and tetrachloroethene (PCE) were identified in the soil. From 1995 to 1997, in situ bioremediation (land farming) was used to treat surface soil, and bioventing was used to treat subsurface soil. Additional investigations to delineate the contaminated soil after the remediation efforts occurred in 1998, 2005, 2007 and 2008. In 2007, multiple soil borings were drilled to 60 feet below ground surface (bgs), and only gasoline range organics (GRO) was identified in the soil at varied concentrations. From 2003 to 2011, groundwater monitoring wells were installed and sampled. TCE was detected above groundwater cleanup levels in Monitoring Well (MW)-2 from 2003-2007. In 2016 Perfluorooctane Sulfonate (PFOS) and Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) were added to the groundwater monitoring program. PFOS and PFOA have been detected below the project action level of 0.4 µg/L but above the EPA Health Advisory level of 0.07 µg/L. Groundwater monitoring is expected to continue at this site.

The U.S. Army HQAES site number is: 02341.1006. Associated sites; Fort Greely Former Fire Training Area BRAC 133 (Hazard ID: 4246) and Fort Greely Former Fire Training Area BRAC 85S (Hazard ID: 1429).

properties.Site_Name: Fort Greely Former Fire Training Area BRAC 133
properties.Problem_Description:
This site is generally known as the Firefighter Training Area, and is investigated under the Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) program as Parcel 133. BRAC Site 133 was used as a firefighter training area from 1975 to 1985. This site contains a grass field, a concrete fill area, and a forested area. The site previously contained a drum storage area and an unlined 6-foot deep pit approximately 20 by 30 feet in size. The burn pit was used to burn waste fuels, oils, solvents, pesticides, paints, and other liquids generated by aircraft and motor maintenance activities. The estimated quantities of waste oil/hydraulic oil and waste fuels burned at the site amount to 19,180 and 2,610 gallons, respectively. Estimated quantities of paints, solvents, and miscellaneous liquids burned amount to 158,400 gallons. Prior to burning, the liquids were stored on site in an unlined and unbermed 55-gallon drum storage area. During initial soil investigations conducted in 1991, contaminants of concern (COCs) identified in the soil were; diesel range organics (DRO), tetrachloroethene (TCE), methylene chloride and antimony. In 1994 and 1997, an in-situ landfarm was constructed and operated to treat soils from the surface to 5 feet below ground surface (bgs). Trenches were excavated, irrigated, turned, and backfilled for two years. In 2010 a soil investigation was conducted to characterize the extent of contamination around the landfarm perimeter berm, and to determine the vertical extent inside the landfarm. DRO and dichlorodiphenyldichloroethane (DDD) were detected in the top two feet of soil above cleanup levels. Soil contamination remains at this site. From 2003 to 2011, groundwater monitoring wells were installed and sampled. TCE was detected above groundwater cleanup levels in Monitoring Well (MW)-2 from 2003-2007. In 2016 Perfluorooctane Sulfonate (PFOS) and Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) were added to the groundwater monitoring program. PFOS and PFOA have been detected below the project action level of 0.4 µg/L but above the EPA Health Advisory level of 0.07 µg/L. Groundwater monitoring is expected to continue at this site.

The U.S. Army HQAES site number is: 02341.1006. Associated sites; Fort Greely Former Fire Training Area BRAC 85N (Hazard ID: 4245) and Fort Greely Former Fire Training Area BRAC 85S (Hazard ID: 1429).

DPW was not notified of the contamination until after concrete had been placed over a portion of the source area.  An unknown area under the concrete containment structure is suspected to be contaminated.  An area east of the slab was screened and sampled.  Further investigation is needed.
