properties.Site_Name: NARL - Sitewide PFAS
properties.Address_1: Near Former NARL Airstrip and Imikpuk Lake
properties.Problem_Description:
This database record includes general information about per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) contamination at the former Naval Arctic Research Laboratory (NARL) in Utqiagvik (formerly Barrow).  

In 2016, the Navy identified Imikpuk Lake as a drinking water source within 1-mile downgradient of a known release of PFAS at the Airstrip site. In 2017, the Navy conducted an investigation of PFAS in Imikpuk Lake; during this investigation, in four out of five surface water samples PFOS and PFOA were detected at concentrations exceeding the United States Environmental Protection Agency lifetime health advisory (LHA) for drinking water of 70 parts per trillion. In September 2017, an advisory was issued to not use Imikpuk Lake as a source of drinking or cooking water. Minimal sampling of soils at the Airstrip and Powerhouse site indicate PFOS present at the Airstrip site above ADEC Cleanup Levels. Currently, the PFAS investigation has been expanded to include assessment and further investigation of eight potential PFAS release areas: three on current Navy property (at the Airstrip Site) and five on transferred property.

2023 Update - All source areas investigated during the SI will continue to the RI phase. These sites include the Airstrip, Powerhouse, and the five sites on transferred property: Former FTA, Building 554, Building 142, Drum Yard, and the Powerhouse Drum Yard.

Upon completion of the investigations, specific areas may be assigned individual Hazard IDs and tracked separately.  Please see site-specific database entries to learn more about an individual NARL PFAS-contaminated site.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB Site 1 South Ramp Spray Test Area AFFF (SS310P)
properties.Address_1: Multiple Areas Near the South Ramp; Including SW Side of Taxiway H
properties.Problem_Description:
This site encompasses multiple areas where per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) have been found near the south ramp of Eielson Air Force Base (EAFB), including the following spills:

Spill no. 16309925602; spill date = 9/12/16; substance = aqueous film forming foam (AFFF);  quantity = 0.25 gallon AFFF + 25 gallons water, no product was recovered; PPRP file no. 107.02.004; description:  AFFF mixed with water and sprayed over area of ~130 square feet.  Fire engine pump system leaked to pavement and grass when being tested. IRP tracking as AOC 17P.

Spill no. 17309907501; spill date = 3/16/17; substance = perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS);  quantity = unknown; PPRP file no. 107.02.004; description:  During geotechnical boring historical contamination was discovered 4 feet below the ground surface. PFOS and arsenic were confirmed in soil above cleanup levels. IRP tracking as AOC 17V.

Taxiway H runs along the northeast side of the ramp. The EAFB fire department has used the paved area of the ramp since the 1980s to perform spray pattern testing on its firefighting equipment. Periodic tests to certify that the spray system on each truck meets minimum performance standards are reportedly conducted on the ramp.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB (AT304) Bldg 4378 AFFF
properties.Problem_Description:
This site is comprised of several releases of aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) from a 15,000-gallon aboveground storage tank (AST) at building 4378 on Eielson Air Force Base.  The site includes the following spills:

Spill no. 16309927401; spill date = 9/30/16; substance = AFFF + water; quantity = 300 gallons; source = 15,000-gallon AST;  PPRP file no. 107.02.004; description:  300 gallons of AFFF mixed with water were released due to valve failure.  Approximately 5 gallons were contained.  IRP tracking as 17O.

Spill no. 16309928002; spill date = 10/6/16; substance = AFFF + water; quantity = 1 gallon; source = 15,000-gallon AST; PPRP file no. 107.02.004; description:  1 gallon of AFFF mixed with water was released due to leaking valve.  IRP tracking as 17O.

properties.Site_Name: JBER-Elmendorf AFFF Area #16 Bldg 6210 UST 249 & OWS
properties.Problem_Description:
A 500-gallon used oil double-walled fiberglass underground storage tank (UST #249), its associated piping, and an oil water separator (OWS) were removed from the ground on August 12, 2016. Excavation activities started with the removal of the fiberglass UST. Staining or odor was not evident in the pea gravel or soil below the excavated tank and groundwater was not encountered during excavation; the excavated tank appeared to be in excellent condition upon removal. 

Samples taken from the bottom of the tank excavation detected trichloroethylene (TCE) above ADEC cleanup levels. Arsenic was also detected above ADEC cleanup levels, but was below the background threshold value for JBER. 

The OWS, located inside the building, was removed from the concrete pad, and the inlet and outlet pipes were plumbed through to the sanitary sewer. The OWS had deteriorated and rusted in areas. Samples were collected from below the outlet pipe, inlet pipes, and bottom of the tank. Chloroform and naphthalene were detected above ADEC cleanup levels. Chloroform was detected and exceeded in the trip blank, but was not detected in any other samples. Naphthalene exceeded ADEC cleanup levels in the sample collected from the middle bottom of the OWS. 

Diesel range organics, residual range organics, and gasoline range organics were also detected in soil at this excavation.

properties.Site_Name: Bloom Enterprises Fire
properties.Problem_Description: On 5/9/17 a spill occurred as a result of fire originating near an incinerator unit where large quantities of used vegetable oil had been stored in plastic containers. The plastic containers melted during the incident, releasing the vegetable oil. In addition, located in the laydown yard where the fire occurred, a few containers of seal coat (a petroleum-based asphalt coating) also melted.  Two fire departments were able to extinguish the fire using aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) and by overhauling the affected infrastructure. Some contamination was contained by creating berms and using a sump to collect the oil/water mixture.  Pooled product was collected using absorbent material, a rope mop skimmer, and a vacuum truck. Recovered liquids were stored in a 10,000-gallon storage tank on site for future treatment and disposal.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB F35A Utiliduct South Loop Extension
properties.Address_1: ~0.25 Mile-Long Area S of Quarry Road, W of Cargain Road, E of Thunderbolt Road
properties.Problem_Description: Between July 12-30, 2018, as part of construction activities for the Eielson Air Force Base F35A Utiliduct South Loop Extension (EIE405), 4.6 million gallons of ground water were collected from a dewatering seep pit and then discharged to the ground surface.  The seep pit is approximately 0.25 mile in length and is located south of Quarry Road, west of Cargain Road, and east of Thunderbolt Road.  The surface discharge point was near the western end of the seepage pit, between man holes 54 and 55.  Analysis of the water discharged confirmed the presence of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) above DEC cleanup levels.  The source of the contaminated groundwater has not been determined.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Gustavus Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description:
The Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities (ADOT&PF) detected perfluoro octanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) in drinking water at two public water system near the airport in Gustavus in July 2018. Concentrations of PFOS+PFOA exceeded the EPA's lifetime health advisory (LHA) level in public water system ID AK 2111476 known as “Gustavus Airport.” Concentrations of PFOS and PFOA were below the Lifetime Health Advisory (LHA) in public water system ID AK 2130596 known as “Gustavus Water System” that provides water to the National Park Service housing and also to the Gustavus School. The contaminants are believed to have originated from the historic use of Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) at various locations at the Gustavus Airport.

The nature and extent of the PFOS and PFOA contamination is still being determined. Quarterly groundwater and drinking water samples are collected by the ADOT. All homes that have drinking water above the EPA LHA are being provided alternate drinking water by the ADOT.  ADOT is working with Department of Administration (DOA) risk management division to install a permanent long term drinking water solution in Gustavus. In 2020, DOA sampled three potential well locations north of the airport on State of Alaska property as potential locations for a public drinking water well. DOA proposes trucking water to impacted homes from the public well. 

For more information visit the ADOT&PF Gustavus webpage:
http://dot.alaska.gov/sereg/GST-AIP_PFA/index.shtml

properties.Site_Name: Residence - 77 Same Old Road Gustavus
properties.Problem_Description: During the groundwater investigation of the Gustavus Airport Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) release as a result of the use of aqueous film forming foam (AFFF), the groundwater at the residence was analyzed for PFAS and the results were above the ADEC cleanup level. Release to ground surface infiltrating to groundwater resulting from fire fighting foam used by the City of Gustavus during a response to a brush fire on 5/18/15.

properties.Site_Name: USCG Air Station Sitka AFFF
properties.Problem_Description:
On 10/26/2018, during a rain event, approximately 100 gallons of water mixed with 3% Chem Guard Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) were released onto the asphalt next to the US Coast Guard (USCG) hangar at the Air Station Sitka.  The release occurred during work on a pull station when an electrical arc caused the fire suppression system to energize and back flush.  Approximately 50 gallons of the AFFF/water mixture were recovered and approximately 50 gallons migrated to a drainage ditch southeast of the hangar which leads to marine water.

Although no data has been collected from the spill path, due to the product spilled, PFAS compounds may be present.  However, due to the site's location on Japonski Island, where there is no groundwater, there is no known immediate threat to human health.

In addition, between 2004 and 2006, An aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) release from the Fire Suppression System (FSS) occurred at the Sitka Air Station.  The AFFF release to the apron from the hangar may have ultimately discharged into the treatment pond located southwest of the hangar. The amount of AFFF released was unknown.

In 2024, USCG conducted a site investigation to determine if PFAS were present in soil, groundwater, or surface water above screening and cleanup levels. Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) were detected above ADEC migration to groundwater cleanup levels in soil. Surface water and groundwater sample results were all below DEC cleanup levels.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB F35A Bldg 6385
properties.Problem_Description:
In August, 2018, during a geotechnical investigation at the site where Building 6385 (Conventional Munitions Facility) is to be constructed (EIE431), one test boring had a solvent odor at ~25 feet below ground surface.  Analysis of soil samples confirm perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and arsenic above DEC cleanup levels.  The source of the contamination is unknown.

A potentially related release was also discovered in May 2020 in the footprint of the former boiler room served by UST 170. The extent of the boiler room spill is not delineated and not confirmed to be from a component of this UST.

See also associated site: Eielson AFB Bldg 6385 UST 170 107.26.053, COC 1-Methylnaphthalene, DRO, Naphthalene. Note this area is outside of the Eielson PFAS plume area. Source area possibly related to the engine-driven fire suppression pumps supplied by the UST at this site.

properties.Site_Name: Alyeska Nordale Storage Yard
properties.Problem_Description: In 2018, the Alyeska Pipeline Service Company (Alyeska) nonpotable water wells known as the east well and the west well were analyzed by EPA method 537M. The drinking water sample results contained Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) above the historic draft ADEC drinking water action level of 0.07 ug/L. This historic draft action level was a summation of five PFAS compounds: PFHpA, PFHxS, PFNA, PFOS and PFOA. In 2019, ADEC's drinking water action level was aligned with the EPA action level. The EPA action level is 0.07 ug/L for the summation of PFOS and PFOA only. The Alyeska Nordale Storage Yard is used by Alyeska for pipeline related equipment and substances. Equipment historically stored onsite includes the Tri-max compressed air foam fire suppression systems (CAFS) containing aqueous film forming foam (AFFF). It is suspected the PFAS is a result of Tri-Max CAFS AFFF releases. It is unknown whether annual Tri-Max CAFS source control fire training drills occurred at the Nordale Yard. This site is located along the Trans Alaska Pipeline corridor at pipeline milepost 460.5.

properties.Site_Name: Clear SFS AFFF Area #5 Sludge Drying Bed/Pit and Leach Field
properties.Problem_Description:
Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) Area #5 Sludge Drying Bed/Pit and Leach Field is located at the northern end of “C” Road. The Sludge Drying Beds/Pit receive waste from the sewage treatment plant and an Imhoff tank/Leach Fields that treated most of the wastewater generated by Clear AFS.

The leach fields are approximately 300 feet southeast of the sludge drying beds/pit. The leach fields are designed to spread out liquid to percolate into the ground, providing a direct pathway to subsurface soil, and after percolation, groundwater. Three leach fields have received sanitary sewage effluent from the Composite Site; however, two are not currently in use because they have reached their capacity to receive sanitary sewage. Leach fields for the Composite Site are able to receive sanitary sewage for approximately 20 years before a new leach field is required. The leach fields have received water captured by the storm drains at several locations where AFFF is known to be stored, including Fire Stations 1 and 2 (Buildings 251 and 250) and the Vehicle Wash Rack (Building 196).

In 2016, USAF conducted a site inspection for five AFFF areas at the Clear Air Force Station. AFFF Area #5 had perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) detections in groundwater up to 0.86 ug/L, exceeding the current (September 2018) Table C cleanup level of 0.40 ug/L.

This site includes spill no. 18309930502, spill date = 11/1/18; substance = Phos-Check fire fighting foam concentrate; quantity = 0.5 gallon; PPRP file no. 151.02.001; Description:  The release occurred at the Vehicle Wash Rack (Building 196) while a fire truck was being washed when some accidentally-activated foam went down the drain that leads to the leach field.  Waste water samples contained PFOA at 0.423 ug/L and Perfluorooctanesulfonic Acid (PFOS) at 0.459 ug/L.

properties.Site_Name: Clear SFS AFFF Area #4 AFFF Spray Test Area (AT030P)
properties.Address_1: SE of Curry Avenue and 5th Street Intersection; Between FT010 ISite 11) and 5th Street
properties.Problem_Description: Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) Area #4 AFFF Spray Test Area is located south and east of the intersection of Curry Avenue and 5th Street on the eastern side of Clear Air Force Station (between FT010 [Site 11] and 5th Street). In 2016, USAF conducted a site inspection for five aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) areas at the Clear Air Force Station. AFFF Area #4  had perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) detections in groundwater up to 2.20 ug/L, exceeding the current (September 2018) Table C cleanup level of 0.40 ug/L.

properties.Site_Name: Clear SFS AFFF Area #3 Fire Station 1 (CD028P)
properties.Address_1: S Side of Clear Highway, ~1,00 ft W of Main Gate; Building 251
properties.Problem_Description: Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) Area #3 - Fire Station 1 (Building 251) is located on the southern side of Clear Highway, approximately 1,500 feet west of the main gate on Clear AFS. Fire Station 1, constructed in 1961, serves as the main fire station for Clear AFS and houses two emergency vehicles that historically carried 25 gallons of AFFF each. In 2016, USAF conducted a site inspection for five AFFF areas at the Clear Air Force Station. AFFF Area #3 had Perfluorooctanesulfonic Acid (PFOS) and Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) detections in soil up to 0.0084 mg/kg and 0.044 mg/kg, respectively, exceeding the current (September 2018) Table B1 Migration to Groundwater cleanup levels of 0.0030 mg/kg for PFOS and 0.0017 mg/kg of PFOA.

properties.Site_Name: Clear SFS AFFF Area #1 Site 11 FT010 (FT010P)
properties.Address_1: SE of Curry Avenue and 5th Street Intersection
properties.Problem_Description: Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) Area #1 (Site 11, FT010) was a 3,500-square-foot fire training pit, located south and east of the intersection of Curry Avenue and 5th Street on the eastern side of Clear Air Force Station. In 2016, USAF conducted a site inspection for five AFFF areas at the Clear Air Force Station. AFFF Area #1 had Perfluorooctanesulfonic Acid (PFOS) and Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) detections in soil up to 0.050 mg/kg and 0.0052 mg/kg, respectively, exceeding the current (September 2018) Table B1 Migration to Groundwater cleanup levels of 0.0030 mg/kg for PFOS and 0.0017 mg/kg of PFOA.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Dillingham Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description:
Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) drinking water well sampling at and adjacent to the Dillingham Airport detected per and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) above DEC action levels. DEC collected 10 drinking water well samples at or adjacent to the airport. Perooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS), perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), and perfluorobutanesulfonate (PFBS) were detected in groundwater at the Holy Rosary Church public water system (AK2263018) at a combined concentration of 185.5 ng/L. Concentrations detected in groundwater from other wells sampled did not exceed DEC action levels. The Holy Rosary Church public water system has been shut down and alternative water is being sourced from a different location. The contaminants are believed to have originated from the historic use of Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) at various locations at the Dillingham Airport.

Two DOT&PF-led follow-up sampling events were conducted in 2019 to investigate the entire area around the Dillingham airport for PFAS compounds. The initial DOT&PF-led sampling reported the combined totals for 5 PFAS compounds and the most recent sampling event reported PFOA and PFOS only as prescribed by the updated April 2019 PFAS Tech Memo. All well owners exceeding their respective Action Level (n = 7) have been contacted and provided an alternative water source. The most recent sampling event showed no new exceedances so the sampling area will not be expanded further. DOT&PF intends to begin a feasibility study into long-term drinking water options for the impacted well owners.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF King Salmon Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description:
Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (ADEC) drinking water well sampling at and adjacent to the King Salmon Airport detected per and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) above ADEC action levels. ADEC collected 9 drinking water well samples at or adjacent to the airport. Perfluoroheptanoic acid, Perfluorohexanesulfonate, and Perfluorooctanoic acid were detected in groundwater at Charlie's Sport Shop at a combined concentration of 154 ng/L. Concentrations detected in groundwater from other wells sampled did not exceed ADEC action levels. The contaminants are believed to have originated from the historic use of Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) at various locations at the King Salmon Airport. 

As of January 2019, investigation is ongoing. The Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities (ADOT&PF) is working with an environmental consulting firm and ADEC to identify and sample other private water wells that may have been affected and develop a long-term alternative water source.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB AFFF Area #1 Air National Guard Hangar Bldg 1171 (SS314P)
properties.Problem_Description: The Eielson Air Force Base Air National Guard (ANG) Hangar (Building 1171) was constructed in 1997, and is equipped with an aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) fire suppression system. The system includes overhead sprinklers and an 800-gallon tank of AFFF concentrate. A minor fire suppression system discharge occurred from a sprinkler in the mechanical room (date unknown), after which a “small amount of foam” was found on the mechanical room floor.  Standard practice for small AFFF spills was to clean up with absorbent pads, which were then taken to Hazardous Materials Storage (Building 3446) for disposal. However, because cleanup documentation for this discharge is not available, it is unknown whether any AFFF was released through the mechanical room door, located on the eastern side of the building.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB AFFF Area #2 Air National Guard KC135 Hangar Bldg 1176 (SS303P)
properties.Problem_Description: The Eielson Air Force Base Air National Guard KC135 Hangar Building 1176 (EP303) hangar was equipped with an aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) fire suppression system that included two foam cannons and an overhead sprinkler system.  However, the hangar was converted to a high-expansion foam (HEF) system (which does not contain Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS)) after 2006. One AFFF release occurred in the mid-1990s when the system activated and reportedly produced 20 (vertical) feet of foam in the hangar (quantity of concentrate unknown). The release was partially contained by floor drains; however, some foam was pushed out the west doors and may have drained to nearby grassy areas.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB AFFF Area #5 Fire Station 1 Bldg 1206 (SS313P)
properties.Problem_Description:
Eielson Air Force Base Fire Station 1 (Building 1206) formerly had a 2,000-gallon aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) underground storage tank (UST) located along the northern side of the building, which was closed in place in 1996. The former AFFF UST was rumored to have foamed over at some time in the past. On October 18, 2016, approximately 10 gallons of an AFFF/water mixture was released from a firefighting truck to pavement and soil on the airfield side of Fire Station 1 during routine testing of firefighting equipment. The nearest drinking well (Well E) is 1,670 feet upgradient (east-southeast) of the location.

With DEC approval, ~50 cubic yards of soil with Perfluorooctanesulfonic Acid (PFOS)-containing AFFF concentrate were excavated and sent to for off-site thermal remediation as an experiment to see if thermal remediation will work for PFOS.

Site was formerly referred to as "Eielson AFB AFFF Area #5 Fire Station 1 Bldg 1206 (EP303)" but updated to reflect Air Force's change in site identifier from EP303 to SS313P.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB Site 3 Former Ball Field Spray Test Area (SS306P)
properties.Problem_Description:
In the 1980s, the Eielson Air Force Base (EAFB) fire department reportedly performed multiple aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) spray pattern tests in an old ball field north of and adjacent to Fire Station #1 (Building 1206). Anecdotal information indicates that
the AFFF may have spread beyond the ball field area. A significant portion of surface water runoff at EAFB enters Garrison Slough.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB Site 4 Foamed Runway (SS312P)
properties.Problem_Description: The North-South runway (Runway 14/32) at Eielson Air Force Base was foamed with aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) as a precautionary measure when a KC135 was preparing to land with potentially disabled landing gear. The landing gear operated correctly, and the aircraft landed without incident.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB AFFF Area #14 Thunderdome Bldg 1140 (SS309P)
properties.Problem_Description:
The Thunderdome hangar (Building 1140) at Eielson Air Force Base is equipped with an aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) fire suppression system that includes two foam cannons and an overhead sprinkler system. The storage tank in the mechanical room holds 1,500 gallons of AFFF concentrate.  Based on historical accounts, there have been two known discharges within the Thunderdome. The first discharge was an intentional demonstration in 1988 or 1989.  The second discharge was an accidental system activation in 2005. During the first discharge, some AFFF was captured by hangar drains, but some also was pushed out hangar doors (it is unknown which doors) and drained into the possible French drain that is connected to an oil-water separator tank (AFCEC, 2015a). The quantities discharged within and outside of the hangar are unknown, although they were both considered “large” (AFCEC, 2015a). Some AFFF may have been washed off the pavement to surrounding
grassy areas.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB Site 2 KC135 Fire (SS311P)
properties.Address_1: Aircraft Parkin Apron, N of Intersection of Taxiways C & F
properties.Problem_Description: In 1989, while shutting down the engines in a KC-135 Stratotanker, an overheated fuel pump exploded causing a fire in the aircraft. An unknown quantity of aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) was used to extinguish the fire. The incident occurred on the aircraft parking apron just north of the intersection of Taxiway C and Taxiway F.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB AFFF Area #4 Fire Training Area (FT009) & Former Base Landfill (LF003)
properties.Address_1: ~1,200 Ft N of Taxiway Refeuling Loop & ~700 Ft E of S End of Runway
properties.Problem_Description:
Fire training exercises at the Fire Training Area (FTA) began in 1955 and historical accounts indicate that the exercises involved burning waste oils, contaminated fuels, and spent solvents. Procedures involved saturating the ground with approximately 5,000 gallons of water, applying fuel, burning the fuel for 30 seconds, and extinguishing it with foam. Aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) use is likely to have occurred starting in the mid-1970s. The previous FTA was replaced by a new, lined fire training facility in 1995.

The landfill was used as the main Base landfill from 1967 to 1987, receiving household garbage, scrap lumber and metal, construction debris, concrete slabs, empty cans, and drums from flightline industrial shops, as well as possibly waste oils, spent solvents, and paint residues and thinners. The subsurface landfill was unlined and contained several excavated areas and trenches for disposal, which reportedly reached below the water table. Potential per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) contamination may be associated with fire training exercises that were reported to have been conducted in the same area as the landfill operations between 1967 and 1976. A historical aerial photograph dated 1959 shows a stained area that is a potential location of a burn pit within the landfill area, separate from the FTA. Additionally, the landfill may contribute to PFAS contamination from other materials containing PFAS within the former main Base landfill.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB AFFF Area #6 Former Adak Bldg Fire (SS302P)
properties.Problem_Description: In 1987 or 1988, a fire occurred at the Former Adak Building. At the time, the building was a warehouse used to store propane and other hazardous materials. The fire reportedly burned for 10 to 12 hours and the building was a total loss. Aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) was used to extinguish the fire. The volume of AFFF used to fight the former Adak Building fire is unknown, but it may have been significant given the amount of time and effort required to extinguish the fire. A previous fire occurred at this location in 1971 and was extinguished with limited damage to the building. The material used to fight the 1971 fire is unknown, but during the early 1970s the amount of AFFF stock was generally limited because stocks of protein foam were used first.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB AFFF Area #7 Former Fire Station 1 (FT092)
properties.Address_1: Traffic Roundabout NE of Bldg 4370, W of Flightline Avenue
properties.Problem_Description:
Former Fire Station 1 was operated in support of flightline activities until approximately 1980, but has subsequently been torn down. Little information is available on construction and operations at the former Fire Station 1, although there have been no known releases of aqueous film forming foam (AFFF).

From the 2024 RIRA: 
The 2017 remedial investigation (RI) fieldwork at Source Areas FT092 and DD097 at Eielson
Air Force Base (AFB), Alaska, was conducted between May and October 2017. The source
areas were investigated together because they entered the investigative process at the same time,
are located within a close proximity on Eielson AFB, and are both subject to the three-party
Federal Facility Agreement (U.S. Air Force [USAF] 1991). The 2017 Remedial
Investigation/Risk Assessment Report for Source Areas FT092 and DD097, Final, Revision 1
was completed in July 2019 (USAF 2019b). The USAF requested revisions for Source
Area DD097 to include a re-screening of analytical results in comparison to U.S. Environmental
Protection Agency regional screening levels and background threshold values, as well as a
screening level ecological risk assessment. Henceforth, all mentions of Source Area FT092 will
be excluded from this revised RI/risk assessment.

Results of the 2016 source evaluations conducted at Source Area DD097 were used to guide RI
field activities. The RI was conducted to determine the physical extents and concentration levels
of contamination; further develop conceptual site models; and provide sufficient quantity and
spatial distribution of data to complete baseline human health risk assessments (HHRAs),
ecological risk assessment (ERA), and supplement future feasibility studies, proposed plans,
and Records of Decision, if required, at this source area.

At Source Area DD097, the drainage ditch immediately north of the corrosion control facility
and the drainage ditch across Loop Access Road were investigated based on anecdotal
information that indicated spent sand blasting material had been dumped into these ditches.
Benzo(a)pyrene was detected above project screening levels in surface soil in the grassy area
adjacent to the corrosion control facility and immediately south and east of the drainage ditch;
these contaminants have been delineated with the exception of a clean boundary north of
DD097 SS15.

Although lead and hexavalent chromium were detected above Alaska Department of
Environmental Conservation human health cleanup levels, the results of the HHRA and ERA
indicate neither of these contaminants nor any other source-area-related analytes pose a risk in
soil or groundwater at Source Area DD097.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB AFFF Area #8 Former Fire Training Area Near Antenna Farm (FT092)
properties.Problem_Description: The former fire training area (FTA) was identified during the 1998 Utilidor investigation. During the investigation locations were identified that were used for fire training exercises during the late 1970s. In addition to two fire training pits near the current Entomology Building, the Assistant Fire Chief indicated that a third area, south of what is now the Antenna Farm, had also been used to burn “unknown liquid wastes” that were accumulated at the location during the week and were then burned during weekend training exercises. The method of extinguishing flames at the former FTA was not indicated, but aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) may have been in use during the late 1970s at Eielson Air Force Base and was therefore likely used in training exercises during that timeframe. The burn areas appear to have been unlined, and if used, AFFF was likely released to the environment. Biosolids land spreading, which could be an additional source of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), also is permitted and may have occurred in this area.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB AFFF Area #9 Former Fire Training Areas Near Entomology Bldg 4335 (FT092)
properties.Problem_Description: Three fire training areas (FTAs) were identified during the 1997 Utilidor investigation. The method of extinguishing the flames in the FTAs were not indicated, but foam, including aqueous film forming foam (AFFF), may have been in use during the late 1970s at Eielson Air Force Base. In addition to fire training activities, drum storage and asphalt mixing also occurred in this vicinity, and several underground storage tanks containing fuels and solvents were found and removed.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB AFFF Area #10 Fuel Pump House Bldg 1246 (SS307P)
properties.Problem_Description: Building 1246 had an aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) system consisting of overhead sprinklers at pumps, a 550-gallon storage tank, and pipeline carrying AFFF to the JP-4 fuel storage tanks. The AFFF system at the fuel pump house was taken out of service at an unknown date after the system was inadvertently activated and AFFF was sent through the under-street piping into the tank farm, containing two JP-4 tanks, and ultimately mixed with the fuel. Protocols for draining the pipes consisted of connecting hoses to the pipeline and draining to dedicated 500-gallon totes, which are then sent to the hazardous materials storage and eventually off-site for disposal.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB AFFF Area #12 Hangar Bldg 1344 (SS305P)
properties.Problem_Description: Around 2000, a system failure resulted in a discharge of aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) concentrate within the mechanical room. The discharge (small, unknown quantity) was contained by the floor drain. One or possibly two larger (quantity unknown) discharges occurred in either 2005 or 2007 and/or 2009. The discharge(s) were described as being partially contained by floor drains, which are connected to the sanitary drains and ultimately lead to the wastewater treatment plant; however, some foam was pushed out the door to the north and may have reached the grassy drainage area to the north of the hangar.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB AFFF Area #15 Wastewater Treatment Plant & Biosolids Land Spreading Area (EP301)
properties.Problem_Description: The waste water treatment plant (WWTP) and Biosolids Land Spreading aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) area consists of multiple areas affected by activities related to management of wastewater and associated biosolids. In addition to sewage, the WWTP currently receives wastewater from drains within hangars that have or have had AFFF systems. As a result, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)-contaminated water from these locations has likely reached the WWTP. The WWTP has drying beds for the biosolids sludge.  After drying, the biosolids are permitted for land spreading in areas around the WWTP and ponds; across Central Avenue from the WWTP; along the northern side of Central Avenue; around the flightline within the fenced area, northeast of the south ramp to Loop Access Road; the area around Outer Loop Road, LF003; and near the WWTP.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Yakutat Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: In February 2019, Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) sampling of potable wells in the immediate vicinity of the Yakutat detected per and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) up to 90 parts per trillion.  The contaminants are believed to have originated from the historic use of Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) at various locations at the Yakutat Airport.

properties.Site_Name: City of Kenai Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: In November 2018, Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) sampling of potable wells in the immediate vicinity of the Kenai municipal airport and Kenai fire training center did not detect concentrations of any per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), with the exception of perfluorohexanoic acid of 0.9 and 0.45 parts per trillion in two wells. There is no screening level for perfluorohexanoic acid. The contaminants are believed to have originated from the historic use of Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) at various locations at the Kenai municipal airport.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Valdez Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: In November 2018, the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) collected water samples of potable wells in the immediate vicinity of the Alaska Department of Transportation & Public Facilities (ADOT&PF) Valdez Pioneer Field airport. Low-level concentrations of per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), were found in three wells; however, none of the detections were above screening levels. The contaminants are believed to have originated from the historic use of Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) at various locations at the Valdez Pioneer Field airport.

properties.Site_Name: Alyeska PS 07 Sitewide PFAS
properties.Address_1: Pump Station 07; Near MP 42 Elliott Highway; Alyeska Pipeline MP 414.2
properties.Problem_Description: In 2018, drinking water samples collected from the onsite potable well at alyeska Pump Station 7 (PS 07) contained perfluorooctanic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS) above EPA lifetime health advisory levels and ADEC Table C groundwater cleanup levels. Monitoring wells advanced adjacent to the drinking water wells also contained PFOA and PFOS above EPA lifetime health advisory levels and ADEC Table C groundwater cleanup levels. The PFOS/PFOA source point is unknown, but expected to be the result of aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) releases. Pump Station 07 (PS07) has a fixed fire suppression system with AFFF to protect critical areas including manifold buildings and other crude process areas. The AFFF PS 07 is stored in the northwest corner of the Shop/Warehouse Building located south of the facility drinking water well. Note: the PS 07 former fire training area is not suspected of being a source. This site is located 1,500 feet downgradient - 100 feet lower than the PS 07 pad. Soil samples collected from the former fire training area have never contained contaminant concentrations above ADEC method two migration to groundwater cleanup levels. See Hazard ID 26733 / file 330.38.143 for more information regarding the former fire training area.

properties.Site_Name: CBJ Hagevig Fire Training Center PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: In June 2019, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) compounds were discovered on site at the City and Borough of Juneau Hagevig Fire Training Center as a result of the use of aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) during regular fire training activities.  Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) was confirmed in soil and ground water above DEC cleanup levels.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Cordova Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Address_1: Mile 13 Copper River Highway; Cordova Airport
properties.Problem_Description: In February 2019, Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) collected water samples from potable wells in the immediate vicinity of the Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities (ADOT&PF) Cordova Airport. Analytical sample results showed that there were no detections of any per- or polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in any of the wells that were sampled.

properties.Site_Name: AIA Anchorage Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description:
Concern over the use of aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) as a fire retardant at the Ted Steven Anchorage International Airport (ANC) has resulted in preliminary investigative sampling performed by AIA personnel for per- or polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). 

The Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting Training Facility (ARFF) has been identified as a source of PFAS with 23,000 parts per trillion (ppt) perfluoroctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) indicated in shallow groundwater, 6,600 ppt in surface water, and 0.18 milligram per kilogram in soil. Sampling indicates the presence of other PFAS sources at ANC not yet identified. Site work for the ARFF building contaminated site will be tracked under file number 2100.38.028.39.

To date groundwater sampling for PFAS at ANC has otherwise included the Fire Training Facility (2100.38.028.26) and well MW-6 at the AIA landspreading area (2100.38.028.03), and drinking water at the Salvation Army Clitheroe Center and Amateur Radio Club. Results were below action levels, or not detected. 

The purpose of this Hazard ID is to document results of sampling activities related to PFAS at AIA. Source areas may be split into individual sites as they are identified.

properties.Site_Name: CBJ Juneau Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: The Juneau International Airport (JIA) is a part of 139 airport and as such, is required to use firefighting foams that meet military specifications, and to test the fire suppression systems periodically.  Although JIA currently uses an aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) that does not contain or break down into perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) or perfluoroctanoic acid (PFOA), historic training activities may have included use of foams containing PFOA, PFOS, and/or other fluorocarbons and their breakdown products.  A per- or polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) investigation is underway.  At this time PFAS has been confirmed above DEC cleanup levels.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Bethel Airport Grant Aviation Plane Crash PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: On July 8, 2019 approximately 80 gallons of a 3% solution of aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) containing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) was released to the ground during aircraft fire at the Bethel airport.  The Grant Aviation aircraft crash-landed and was on an unpaved area adjacent to the runway when the foam was applied to the fire.

properties.Site_Name: Nome Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description:
The Alaska Army National Guard (AKANG) completed a preliminary assessment for per- or polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) at the Nome Army Aviation Operating Facility at the Nome Airport. The preliminary assessment indicated that current and former AKANG activities did not contribute to potential PFAS contamination in the AKANG facility and adjacent area. The preliminary assessment also indicated that the Nome Airport Fire Department Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) Spray Area and the Nome Airport Fire Department may be sources of PFAS contamination. Analytical sampling was not completed.

The purpose of this Hazard ID is to document investigative and characterization activities related to PFAS at the Nome Airport facility. Source areas may be split into individual Hazard IDs if they are identified.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Bethel Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Address_1: Bethel Airport; Chief Eddie Hoffman Highway
properties.Problem_Description:
The Alaska Army National Guard (AKANG) completed a preliminary assessment for per- or polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) at the Bethel Army Aviation Operating Facility at the Bethel Airport. The preliminary assessment indicated that current and former AKANG activities did not contribute to potential PFAS contamination in the AKANG facility and adjacent area. The preliminary assessment also indicated that the Bethel Airport Fire Department and the Skyvan Crash area may be sources of PFAS contamination. Analytical sampling was not completed.

During summer 2020, ADOT conducted geotechnical drill across both runways in preparation for reconstruction in 2021. Soil samples were collected at each drilling location and tested for PFOA and PFOS.  PFOA and PFOS were widely detected across the entire Bethel Airport at concentrations below the ADEC cleanup levels. PFOS exceeded the 3.0 µg/kg cleanup level in two test borings along Runway 1L/19R between Taxiways D and the intersection with Runway 12/30 at 13 and 25 µg/kg. PFOA exceeded the 1.7 µg/kg cleanup level in one test boring on Taxiway D. 

The purpose of this Hazard ID is to document investigative and characterization activities related to PFAS at the Bethel Airport facility. Source areas may be split into individual Hazard IDs if they are identified.

properties.Site_Name: City of North Pole Fire Station PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: During summer 2018, DEC sampled a selection of monitoring wells and private wells in North Pole, down gradient from the former refinery. While per- or polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) were widely detected, all Perfluorooctanesulfonic Acid (PFOS) & Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) combined results were below 70 parts per trillion (ppt), except for monitoring well MW-316, located along Cross Way, just downgradient of the City of North Pole's Fire Station. At the 15-foot depth interval, this well had PFOS & PFOA concentration of 1,070 ppt (and a total detected PFAS concentration of 4,341 ppt, with a Perfluorononanoic Acid PFNA concentration of 2,400 ppt), suggesting a release had occurred upgradient. During 2020, onsite investigations confirmed PFAS was present in both soil and groundwater above cleanup levels. PFOS and PFOA are present in soil at 7.4 and 9.1 mg/kg, respectively. PFOS and PFOA are present in groundwater at 140,000J and 2,100 ng/L, respectively. Additional sampling effort for further delineation and private well/monitoring well/surface water sampling is pending.

properties.Site_Name: Petro Star Valdez Refinery Truck Rack PFAS
properties.Problem_Description:
On July 11, 2019 a tanker truck exploded at the Petro Star Valdez Refinery truck rack while loading diesel fuel. Fire fighting crews used an aqueous film forming foam (AFFF)/water solution to extinguish the fire. The diesel, AFFF, and water solution drained to the northeast side of the facility perimeter with some escaping through an open canal valve. The substance that went through the canal valve followed a drainage that leads to Abercrombe Creek. An emergency berm was constructed to restrict the flow of the substance, but some may have escaped the emergency containment.  Initial site characterization sample analysis confirmed the following contaminants in soil above DEC cleanup levels:  diesel range organics, 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene, 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene, naphthalene, benzene, ethylbenzene, and xylenes; as well as perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA)  Additionally, PFOS and PFOA were confirmed in surface water above the DEC cleanup levels.

In the Fall of 2019, contaminated soil was excavated within the impacted area to a depth of two feet below ground surface (bgs) except for the area between the culvert outlet and the emergency dike where soil was excavated to a depth of one foot bgs.  The total volume of soil excavated and stockpiled was estimated at approximately 3,050 cubic yards.

Analysis of post excavation samples confirm PFOS and PFOA remain above DEC cleanup levels, both inside and outside the facility perimeter.

On June 27, 2022, another tanker truck caught on fire at the Petro Star Valdez Refinery fuel truck loading rack.  It is estimated that 5000 gallons of diesel was released, of which much burned up from the fire.  In addition, an oily fire foam water was released to douse the fire, most of which was recovered.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Cold Bay Airport Abandoned Fire Station
properties.Address_1: Intersection of North Apron Road and Reeve Avenue
properties.Problem_Description:
The Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities (ADOT&PF) conducted a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment (ESA) at the abandoned fire house at the Cold Bay airport in 2019. Historic as-built from 1959 indicate two floor drains in the main building. Due to the dilapidated building still on site, the floor drains status was not determined during the Phase I ESA. Three electrical transformers were observed in the northwest quarter of the property. Fuel supply lines were found on the south side of the former fire station, but no tanks were observed. It is suspected that a 1,000-gallon underground storage tank (UST) used for heating oil is on site. Twelve 5-gallon containers of aqueous film forming foams were present in the dilapidated building. A metal vault filled with storm water was found near the concrete foundation. The purpose of vault is unknown. 

In 2014 fourteen 55-gallon drums were removed from the former fire and crash station. One drum of used oil was reported to have leaked petroleum from an open bung hole. The property has been unoccupied since 1996 and ADOT&PF was reportedly the sole occupant of the site since the building was operated the by the U.S. government. The fire house was reportedly taken out of service in 1996 when a new offsite fire facility was constructed.

Limited sampling was done in 2019. Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) was found below ADEC cleanup levels at concentrations of 0.0030 mg/kg and 0.0011 mg/kg in surface soil. Diesel range organics (DRO) of 2,650 mg/kg was measured in the surface soil and mercury of 1.79 mg/kg. Both DRO and mercury are above ADEC cleanup levels. Contaminants of potential concern at the site are DRO, residual range organics (RRO), volatile organic compounds (VOCs), polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), Perfluorooctanesulfonic Acid (PFOS), Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA), and mercury.

properties.Site_Name: ConocoPhillips West Sak SWPT #1 Fire Training Area PFAS
properties.Address_1: 2 Miles East of Kuparuk Operations Unit
properties.Problem_Description: Prior to being a fire training area, one oil well was drilled at the West Sak Single Well Production Test (SWPT) #1 pad in 1983 and operated until 1985. The site was utilized for fire training activities at Kuparuk after 1985. From 1985 to 1986, diesel was ignited in a steel tank placed directly on the gravel pad for fire training purposes. Around 1987, a synthetic lined gravel burn pit was installed at the northwest end of the SWPT pad for additional fire training activities. In 1989, a synthetic-lined containment pond was added to the southeast of the burn pit to contain the fire-fighting water runoff. By 1993, all fire-training activities had been moved to the lined area. A new state-of-the-art liner and sump were installed in the central portion of the pad in 1997. Potential run-off from the area at the north end of the pad was monitored. In 2001, a Reserve Pit Closure Plan was submitted to ADEC and pit closure was granted on September 14, 2001.   Fire training using firefighting foam within the triple-lined bermed area began at the site in 1994 and was discontinued in 2014.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Iliamna Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: In June 2020, the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) collected water samples of private and public wells in the immediate vicinity of the Iliamna airport. Low-level concentrations of per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), were found in multiple wells; however, none of the detections were above screening levels. The contaminants are believed to have originated from the historic use of Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) at various locations at the Iliamna airport.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Aniak Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: In March 2020, the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) collected water samples of private and public wells in the immediate vicinity of the Aniak airport. Low-level concentrations of per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), were found in multiple wells; however, none of the detections were above screening levels. The contaminants are believed to have originated from the historic use of Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) at various locations at the Aniak airport.

properties.Site_Name: UAF MAPTS Fire Control Systems AFFF
properties.Problem_Description: Some time in 2018, approximately 1,000 gallons of aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) were released to the ground from a storage tank at Fire Control Systems, Inc. property on Commerce Avenue in Kenai.  The spilled product was owned by the University of Alaska Fairbanks (UAF), for use by the Mining and Petroleum Training Service Center of Excellence (MAPTS), at the time of its release and had been stored on this property for many years.  The cause of the release was reportedly from a damaged site glass on the tank.  The release was not reported until 6/28/2019.  Prior to the spill being reported to DEC, a contractor was hired to dispose of the remaining product and excavate the source area.  8 drums and 4 supersacks of soil were excavated and later approved for transport and disposal.  When soil impacts were greater than expected another contractor was hired to begin site characterization activities.  A site characterization workplan  was submitted in late 2019 and approved on 2/11/2020.  DEC sampled the on-site well on 1/30/2020 and the sample results yielded non-detect for per- and polyfluorinated substances (PFAS).  In the summer of 2020, additional site activities occurred, including soil borings and monitoring well installations.  A subsequent report indicated that groundwater has been impacted and further delineation is necessary.

properties.Site_Name: Fire Control Systems PFAS Kenai
properties.Problem_Description:
There appear to have been multiple releases at the Fire Control Systems property on Commerce Avenue in Kenai.

A release of approximately 1,000 gallons of aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) from a storage tank occurred sometime in 2018.  The spilled product was owned by the University of Alaska Fairbanks (UAF) for use by the Mining and Petroleum Training Service Center of Excellence (MAPTS).

In the summer of 2020, additional site activities occurred in relation to the 2018 spill, including soil borings and monitoring well installations.  A subsequent report indicated that groundwater has been impacted and further delineation is necessary.  This site is being tracked as informational. 
The contaminated site will be documented separately under site record: Hazard ID 27287; file no. 2320.38.085; UAF MAPTS Fire Control Systems AFFF.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Cordova Airport ARFF Bldg
properties.Address_1: Mile 13 Copper River Highway; Cordova Airport
properties.Problem_Description: In July 2020, site characterization activities were conducted at the existing Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting Building (ARFF) at the Cordova Airport in preparation for removal and replacement of the existing ARFF with a Combined Maintenance Facility to include a Snow Removal Equipment Building (SREB) and a new ARRF.  Initial sample results confirmed the presence of petroleum compounds in soil and Perfluorooctanesulfonic Acid (PFOS) in soil and ground water.  The petroleum contamination is located in the vicinity of an out-of-use underground heating oil tank and the PFOS contamination is suspected to be from releases of aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) possibly from system testing or training activities.

properties.Address_1: Juneau Airport, 1873 Shell Simmons Drive, W of CCFR Glacier Station 3 at 1700 Crest Avenue
properties.Problem_Description: On April 21, 2021, approximately 2.25 gallons of Ansulite AFC-3MS-C, 3% Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) concentrate mixed with 200-300 gallons of water were accidentally released to the ground when the foam release button was left on during a weekly check of Capital City Fire Rescue (CCFR) aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicle (ARFF) A3.  The release occurred at the City and Borough of Juneau (CBJ) International Airport, just west of CCFR Glacier/Airport Station 3 and ~20 yards north of Jordan Creek.  The estimated surface area affected was 20 x 40 square yards.

During a routine monitoring event, Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities (ADOT&PF) detected an exceedance of the EPA lifetime health advisories (LHA) for perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) at a monitoring well (identified as MW-2-20) located on the west side of the Salmon River.

properties.Site_Name: U.S. Ecology Moose Creek Facility
properties.Problem_Description:
The Moose Creek OIT Facility is a thermal remediation facility for contaminated soils and other related materials. PFOS was detected in a water sample from the treatment facility main water supply well in March, 2016 at 1.3 micrograms per liter (ug/l), which exceeds the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Provisional Health Advisory level of 0.07 µg/l for drinking water and also the ADEC cleanup level of 0.4 µg/l. 

In 2016, a Site Assessment was performed to sample pre-2016 soil stockpiles, fly ash stockpiles, treated soil discharge areas, and water samples from the on-site treatment facility supply well. Both of the groundwater results exceeded the ADEC Cleanup Level for PFOS (0.4 milligrams/L) at concentrations of 1.04 and 1.07 milligrams/L, respectively. Additionally, seven of the 14 soil sample results exceeded the ADEC MTGW CUL of 3 micrograms per milligram for PFOS, at concentrations ranging from 5.57 to 32.9 micrograms per milligram. 

In 2023 the Moose Creek Facility South Contaminated Soil Storage Pad (Pad B-Phase 1) Decommissioning Interim Report identified exceedances of DEC migration to groundwater cleanup level for PFOS and PFOA in soil.

properties.Site_Name: Fort Yukon LRRS Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description:
In September 2021, laboratory results of the drinking water well at Fort Yukon Long Range Radar Station (LRRS) revealed levels of per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) above the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA's) Lifetime Health Advisory level (LHA) for total combined levels of perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic (PFOA) in drinking water. PFOA concentrations were detected at a maximum value of 102 ng/L, or 102,000 ppt in untreated/unfiltered water, exceeding the LHA of 70 ppt. The well is located approximately one mile upgradient (east) of the Fort Yukon City drinking water well. As of September 2021, the USAF provided alternate water in the form of bottled water to staff at the LRRS; alternate water will be provided until DEC confirms it is no longer needed. Further investigation is ongoing to determine the source of PFAS, the extent of contamination, and necessary treatment for the installation.  

The city's drinking water well was also sampled in September of 2021 and all sample results were non-detect for PFOS/PFOA.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Wrangell Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: In May 2022, the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) collected water samples of private and public wells in the vicinity of the Wrangell airport. Low-level concentrations of per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), were found in multiple wells; however, none of the detections were above screening levels. The contaminants are believed to have originated from the historic use of Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) at various locations at the Wrangell airport.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB TU108
properties.Address_1: Near south loop taxiway access road
properties.Problem_Description: During the 2021 Phase II Source Evaluation, 15 soil samples were collected from five soil borings and five temporary monitoring wells were installed and sampled at TU108. Results indicated naphthalene, alpha BHC, and hexavalent chromium exceeded ADEC soil cleanup levels. Metals in groundwater including arsenic and manganese exceed Eielson background concentrations. Cobalt, iron and lead exceed EPA Residential Soil Regional Screening Levels.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB DA112
properties.Problem_Description: During the initial walk through of the site, multiple tar seeps were identified across the site. The tar seeps ranged in size, were tacky to the touch, and had a slight tar odor to them. Surface dumping of asphalt or asphalt byproducts is the suspected source of contamination at Site DA112. The tar is confirmed to have contaminated soils with concentrations of DRO and naphthalene above ADEC cleanup levels.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB SR109
properties.Address_1: Near corner of Wabash Ave and North St.
properties.Problem_Description: During the 2021 Phase II Source Evaluation, 15 samples were collected from 15 soil borings and five temporary monitoring wells were installed and sampled at Site SR109. Concentrations of naphthalene in soil and PFOS in soil and groundwater exceed ADEC cleanup levels. Concentrations of PCB Arochlor 1260 and Arochlor 1254 exceed EPA Regional Screening Levels in soil.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB TU105
properties.Address_1: approximately 600 feet southwest of the Richardson HWY Milepost 338
properties.Problem_Description: During the 2021 Phase II Source Evaluation, 15 soil samples were collected from five soil borings and five temporary monitoring wells were installed and sampled at Site TU105. Results indicated two pesticides, alpha-BHC and beta-BHC, exceeded ADEC soil cleanup levels. The primary source and release mechanism for contaminants at Site TU105 is widespread use of pesticides at Eielson AFB.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB SS110
properties.Address_1: near north end of Central Ave. on east side of roadway
properties.Problem_Description: During the 2021 Phase II Source Evaluation, 15 soil samples were collected from five soil borings and five temporary monitoring wells were installed and sampled at Site SS110. Results indicate 1-methylnaphthalene, 2-methylnaphthalene and naphthalene exceeded ADEC cleanup level in soil. PCB Arochlor 1254 and molybdenum exceeded the EPA Residential Soil Levels. PFOS was present in groundwater at concentrations exceeding 70 parts per trillion. Arsenic exceeded ADEC cleanup levels in groundwater.

properties.Site_Name: Fort Wainwright Biosolids Application Field
properties.Address_1: 0.3 miles SW of 2079 Montgomery Road, Ft. Wainwright, AK
properties.Problem_Description: The Fort Wainwright Biosolids Application Field is located to the southeast of Ladd Army Airfield (LAAF), approximately 0.3 miles from the Chena River on Fort Wainwright, Alaska and was used to spread biosolids generated from the Golden Heart Utilities’ wastewater treatment facility. The volume of biosolids and the exact dates of application are unknown. During the August 2020 site investigation, three shallow soil samples and one groundwater sample were collected. Perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) was detected in soil at a maximum concentration of 0.048 mg/kg. A monitoring well was also sampled downgradient of this site but no exceedances of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) were encountered. A supplemental SI or remedial investigation is needed to delineate the PFAS contamination at this site.

properties.Site_Name: Fort Wainwright Fire Station #2
properties.Problem_Description:
The Fire Station #2 (Building 4390) is located along Neely Road in Fort Wainwright, Alaska, south of the Bassett Army Community Hospital.  An inventory from 2020 indicated that aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) was being stored at the Fire Station #2 in mobile equipment. The dates of storage at this location are not known. The Fire Station #2 is located in an industrial/commercial use area; however, several residential use areas surround the site. Ground cover at the site includes gravel, grass, and pavement. Fire Station #2 is approximately 0.3 mile from the Chena River. 

During a site investigation conducted in August 2020, two shallow soil samples and three groundwater samples were collected. Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) was detected in the shallow soil samples, but fell below migration to groundwater cleanup level found in 18 AAC 75.341, Table B2. Perfluorobutane sulfonic acid (PFBS) was detected in the groundwater at a concentration of 6,500 nanograms per liter (ng/L). The detected concentration of PFBS exceeded the EPA's tapwater regional screening level. Due to the proximity of the groundwater contamination to the Chena River, there is potential migration to surface water, with potential impacts to eco receptors and humans. A supplemental site inspection or remedial investigation is needed to delineate the per-and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) contamination at this site.

properties.Site_Name: Fort Wainwright Neely Road Fire Training Area
properties.Problem_Description:
The training area is located along Neely Road in Fort Wainwright, Alaska, south of the Bassett Army Community Hospital. The training area is composed of a gravel lot between the hospital and the education center building (Building 4391) to the east of the Fire Station #2 (Building 4390) and was used to stage a helicopter fuselage fire simulator for the training activities. The frequency of firefighting training activities performed here is unknown. Evidence of foam expelled on the gravel ground surface during firefighter training activities were reported and documented in 2011. This training area is located in an industrial/commercial use area; however, several residential use areas surround the site. Ground cover at the site includes gravel, grass, and pavement. The adjacent training area is approximately 0.3 mile from the Chena River. 

During a site investigation conducted in August 2020, two shallow soil samples and three groundwater samples were collected. Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) was detected in the shallow soil samples, but fell below migration to groundwater cleanup level found in 18 AAC 75.341, Table B2. Perfluorobutane sulfonic acid (PFBS) was detected in the groundwater at a concentration of 6,500 nangograms per liter (ng/L). The detected concentration of PFBS exceeded the EPA's tapwater regional screening level. Due to the proximity of the groundwater contamination to the Chena River, there is potential migration to surface water, with potential impacts to eco receptors and humans. A supplemental site inspection or remedial investigation is needed to delineate the per-and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) contamination at this site.

properties.Site_Name: Fort Wainwright Fire Training Area Near Bldg 2420
properties.Address_1: 0.25 miles SE of Engineer Lake off of Old Badger Road
properties.Problem_Description: The Fire Training Area is located near Building 2420 in the southeast portion of Fort Wainwright, Alaska (FWA). This site is a fenced lot which slopes slightly to the east and was used for firefighting training activities. It is approximately 0.25 miles from Engineer Lake and 2 miles from the Chena River. There is a known release of approximately 20 gallons of aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) concentrate in the southeastern portion of this lot between 2013 and 2014. Three shallow soil samples and one groundwater sample were collected at the site. Perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) was detected in soil samples with a maximum concentration of 0.0090 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg) and no exceedances were detected in groundwater. A supplemental site inspection or remedial investigation is needed to delineate the per-and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) contamination at this site.

properties.Site_Name: Fort Wainwright Taxiway D
properties.Address_1: Taxiway East of Fire Station #1, West end of Ladd Army Airfield runways
properties.Problem_Description: Taxiway D is located near the center of Ladd Army Airfield (LAAF) between Fire Station #1 and the runway. This taxiway was used for firefighter training activities in 2013 and 2014 while the new LAAF Hangar 4 was being constructed. During this time, aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) was sprayed from fire trucks and allowed to dissipate and dry on the tarmac. Former FWA personnel indicated that cumulative use of AFFF concentrate used was approximately 200 gallons. The Taxiway D boundary does not overlap with any Installation Restoration Program sites. It is surrounded by paved runways and grass cover. The Chena River is approximately 0.5 miles downgradient of this taxiway and may be a complete migration to surface water pathway.  Perfluorooctanesulfonate (PFOS) contamination was confirmed in surface soil [0.072 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg)] and groundwater [58 nanograms per liter (ng/L)]. Surface water along Clear Creek had PFOS and PFOA concentrations of 880 ng/L and 69 ng/L respectively. A supplemental site inspection or remedial investigation is needed to delineate the per-and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) contamination at this site.

properties.Site_Name: Fort Wainwright Taxiway E
properties.Address_1: Taxiway West of Firestation #1, West end of LAAF runways.
properties.Problem_Description: Taxiway E is located on the west end of Ladd Army Airfield (LAAF) on Fort Wainwright, Alaska (FWA). This taxiway was used for firefighter training activities in 2013 and 2014 while the new LAAF Hangar 4 was being constructed. During this time, aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) was sprayed from fire trucks and allowed to dissipate and dry on the tarmac. Former FTWW personnel indicated that cumulative use of AFFF concentrate during this time was approximately 200 gallons between Taxiways E and D. It is surrounded by paved runways and grass cover. The Chena River is approximately 0.25 mile downgradient of this taxiway and may be a complete migration to surface water pathway. During a site investigation (SI) conducted in August 2020, perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic sulfonic acid (PFOA) contamination was confirmed in surface soil, groundwater, and surface water. Contamination was confirmed in the soil and groundwater. The maximum concentrations in the soil were determined to be 2 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg) (PFOS) and 0.004 mg/kg (PFOA). The maximum concentration in groundwater of were found to be 340 nanograms per liter (ng/L) (PFOS) and 77 ng/L (PFOA). Surface water along Clear Creek had PFOS and PFOA concentrations of 880 ng/L and 69 ng/L respectively A supplemental site investigation or remedial investigation is needed to delineate the per-and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) contamination at this site.

properties.Site_Name: ADOT&PF Deadhorse Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: In June 2022, a site investigation occurred as part of the planning process for airport improvements at the Deadhorse Airport. Near surface soil samples were taken around culverts and areas of potential contamination. PFOS and Benzene detections exceeded the migration to groundwater cleanup levels. The site was not fully delineated as sampling locations were specific to areas where soil was to be excavated  or disturbed during construction.

properties.Site_Name: Eielson AFB Basewide PFAS - Township 2S, Range 3E, Sec 29, Portion of Lots 4 and 16, FNSB PAN 646661
properties.Address_1: Township 2S, Range 3E, Sec 29, Portion of Lots 4 and 16
properties.Problem_Description: This Hazard ID has been entered in Informational status because of the application of an environmental covenant due to contamination from the following site: Hazard ID 26773 - Eielson AFB Basewide (AKA Sitewide) PFAS. The property is underlain by per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS) in groundwater. The environmental covenant describes activity and use limitations for the property, based on remaining contamination making it safe for some, but not all, uses.

properties.Site_Name: Galena AFS BRAC Landfarm
properties.Address_1: Former Campion AFS airstrip, approximately 6 miles southeast of Galena
properties.Problem_Description:
The US Air Force Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) landfarm is located on the former Campion AFS runway, approximately six miles southeast of Galena. The landfarm was initially designed and constructed in 2012 to stockpile and treat petroleum-contaminated soil excavated from Sites SS005, AST1569, SS014, SS017, and OT099. The landfarm was subsequently expanded in 2013 and 2018. Several thousand cubic yards of contaminated soil is stockpiled in the north and south stockpiles, awaiting treatment. Groundwater sampling has been conducted at the northeastern end of the landfarm since 2013. DRO and RRO have exceeded the Table C groundwater cleanup levels since 2013 and 2016, respectively.

In May 2025, the USAF shared preliminary results from the landfarm sampling event, indicating perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) is present in exceedance of the applicable 18 AAC 75 Table B1 cleanup levels sourced from aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) impacted soil. Other per and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are present above EPA Regional Screening Levels (RSLs). In June 2025, DEC sent a letter restricting the addition of stockpiled soil to the landfarm, and no soil was to be removed for reuse unless analytical data are submitted to demonstrate no PFAS are present above regulatory cleanup levels.

properties.Site_Name: McGrath Airport Sitewide PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: A well search and sampling effort was conducted at the McGrath airport to evaluate PFAS impacts. PFOS, PFOA and other PFAS were detected in groundwater at concentrations below the DEC action level.

properties.Problem_Description: In support of construction planning, sampling was conducted in January 2020.  PFAS were detected above cleanup levels in soil and groundwater. The site is near Postmark Bog, which is known to have PFAS contamination; however, a different source is likely.
