properties.Site_Name: Alaska Airlines Facility Maintenance AIA
properties.Problem_Description: On March 2, 2022, a discharge consisting of approximately 1,100 gallons of Ansulite 3% Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) and 35,000 gallons of water occurred at or near the Alaska Airlines cargo hangar. An unknown quantity of this mixture discharged into the floor drain connected to the Anchorage Waste & Water Utility treatment plant. The remaining fluid flowed outside of the building onto paved areas around the west side of the building and into drainage ditches to the north along Old International Airport Road. Snow and ice on the paved area surrounding the building and along approximately 1,500 feet of drainage ditch were recovered by U.S. Ecology and placed into two snow piles within a containment area inside the structure located southeast of the main facility. Samples from snow pile melt water and surrounding drainage ditches were collected and had PFAS concentrations exceeding ADEC groundwater cleanup levels.

properties.Site_Name: ARNG Bethel AAOF
properties.Address_1: Army National Guard Bethel Army Aviation Operating Facility
properties.Problem_Description: The Army National Guard (ARNG) Bethel Army Aviation Operating Facility (AAOF) is equipped with an aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) fire suppression system which is supplied by two 800-gallon tanks. One of the tanks has a leaky sight gauge and has been serviced twice in the last ten years, producing less than 1 quart of AFFF each servicing event. Additionally, several Tri-Max fire extinguishers were found in the Bethel AAOF, although no records of their maintenance or use were found. After a Site Inspection in September 2021 in which 7 soil borings (21 primary soil samples) were advanced and completed as monitoring wells (7 primary groundwater samples), multiple PFAS compounds were detected in soil and groundwater. Only PFOA exceeded current DEC cleanup levels in soil, and there were no exceedances in groundwater above current DEC cleanup levels.

properties.Site_Name: Nikiski Former KPB Fire Station
properties.Problem_Description:
PFOS and PFOA were detected above the drinking water action level in source water wells for the Nikishka Bay Public Water System in late 2023. The source of the PFAS contamination is currently unknown.  In early 2023, a project was conducted which included a drinking water well search, public outreach, collecting drinking water samples, laboratory analysis of the drinking water samples and reporting. Sixteen samples were collected and analyzed. The drinking water samples did not contain PFOS or PFOA.  However, PFHxS was detected in two wells and PFHxa was detected in one well at concentrations less than EPA regulatory limits. PFHpA and PFHxA were detected above the reporting limit in one sample, however, DEC and the EPA do not have regulatory or drinking water action levels for the analytes.

Site assessment activities were completed in 2024 on behalf of DEC in the vicinity of the Kenai Spur Highway and Nikishka Beach Road in Nikiski. The characterization activities included advancement of 8 soil borings, installation of 3 monitoring wells, and the collection of soil and groundwater samples in order to assess the extent of per- and polyfluororalkyl substances as well as trichloroethylene. Analytical results indicate that PFAS constituents were present in both surface and subsurface soil samples from six of the eight soil borings and in each of the groundwater samples at concentrations
above ADEC and/or EPA screening levels. Tetrachloroethene was present in groundwater in one of the monitoring wells at a concentration above the ADEC and EPA screening levels.

properties.Site_Name: Commercial Property - 11151 Calaska Circle
properties.Problem_Description: During a due diligence investigation for a potential property sale of a former 3M warehouse, PFAS and PFOA compounds were identified in the soil and groundwater. The compounds are believed to be associated with a release of fire suppressant. The amount and date of release are unknown.

properties.Site_Name: Hilcorp Construction Camp 2A Fire Training Ground
properties.Address_1: NE corner of Construction Camp 2A in Western Operating Area
properties.Problem_Description:
Fire training activities at Construction Camp 2A (CC2A) were reported to have been conducted
once per week for six years. Foaming chemicals used were either aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) in a 3 percent solution, or AFFF/alcohol type concentrate (ATC) in 3 to 6 percent solutions. The preliminary site investigation activities were performed in June, July, August, and September 2019. Six soil borings were completed, and six monitoring wells were installed outside the CC2A site liner. Soil and water samples were collected and analyzed, and pad porewater elevation data was collected. Analytical results for soil samples collected from the six soil borings indicated PFOA/PFOS were not present at concentrations above their respective ADEC cleanup levels for Arctic Zone soils in 2021. Analytical results for pad porewater samples collected for PFOA were reported at concentrations below the ADEC cleanup levels (0.40 micrograms per liter [µg/L]) in all the monitoring wells. The highest concentration of PFOA was 0.34 µg/L at MW-03 on the west side of the liner.  Analytical results for pad porewater samples collected for PFOS were reported at concentrations above the ADEC CL (0.40 µg/L) in all the monitoring wells. The highest concentration of PFOS was at MW-03 at 40 µg/L.

properties.Site_Name: Sparrevohn LRRS AT009P Fire Training & General Lower Camp Area
properties.Problem_Description: At this time the source of per- and polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) at Sparrevohn LRRS is unknown. The suspected source is fire training activities/historical activities at the site conducted between the 1950s and early 2000s. Sparrevohn LRRS is a remote installation where a PFAS Remedial Investigation (RI) is currently being conducted. The purpose of the PFAS RI is to delineate the nature and extent of PFAS. During a 2020 Preliminary Assessment and 2022 Site Inspection (SI) at the site PFOS was detected in groundwater and soils at the site of suspected fire training and the general lower camp area during the PFAS SI. The extent is not fully characterized at this time.

properties.Site_Name: Indian Mt. LRRS Former Vehicle Maint Shop (SS012P)
properties.Address_1: 15 miles east of Hughes; Indian Mountain
properties.Problem_Description:
The Indian Mountain Long Range Radar Station (LRRS) former vehicle maintenance shop SS012P (VMS) is located approximately 15 miles east of Hughes, Alaska. The former VMS operated in 1976 and was identified as an area where aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) was stored. The available site information indicates that the area was primarily used for fire truck storage, filling, test spray, and maintenance. The site now has a storage building built on top of the building footprint. 

In 2020 a site inspection was conducted at Indian Mountain LRRS to determine the extent of possible PFAS contamination at the installation. The former VMS was included in this investigation. Several contaminants exceeded the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (ADEC) action level in groundwater samples collected. Contaminants were also detected in soil and surface water samples, but concentrations were below action levels.

Additional site characterization was conducted in 2024 to further characterize the PFAS detected in the 2020 site inspection. The results are pending. Current potential exposure pathways include groundwater ingestion; however, no groundwater currently is used as drinking water at Indian Mountain LRRS. Therefore, exposure is limited at this site. The site has been recommended for further remedial investigation to fully characterize the extent of the contamination.

properties.Site_Name: USCG Kodiak LOWS Facility - Bldg N56
properties.Problem_Description:
During fieldwork operations by USCG to support the Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) Site Investigation (SI), a visible oil sheen was observed. The work included sampling around the Liquid Oily Waste Facility (Building N56) which is adjacent to the steam plant.

A petroleum/fuel odor and a visible oil sheen were encountered in the soil interval from 5 to 12 feet below the ground surface. Photoionization Detector (PID) readings determined that further site assessment is required to fully characterize the site.

properties.Site_Name: Cape Romanzof LRRS - Sitewide
properties.Problem_Description:
This site has been entered to track multi-site reviews and administrative actions for all of Cape Romanzof's contaminated sites. See specific file numbers starting with 2526.38 for information regarding specific sites at Cape Romanzof.

Cape Romanzof Long Range Radar Site (LRRS) is in the Yukon-Kuskokwim region of Alaska, at the western end of the Askinuk Mountains and on a small peninsula that extends into the Bering Sea. The LRRS is approximately 540 air miles west of Anchorage, 165 miles northwest of Bethel, and 170 miles southeast of Nome. The USAF property at the installation encompasses about 4,900 acres of land situated within the boundaries of the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta National Wildlife Refuge, a federally protected habitat area. The Cape Romanzof installation comprises two main areas: the Lower Camp and the Upper Camp. The Lower Camp lies at the head of a valley next to tundra fields and ephemeral streams, and the Upper Camp is situated at the top of Towak Mountain.

The Cape Romanzof LRRS was one of the 10 original aircraft control and warning sites in the Alaska Air Defense System. Installation construction was completed in 1952 and operations began in 1953. The White Alice Communication Station, which replaced the original communication and warning system, became operational in 1958. By 1977, Cape Romanzof LRRS was operating as a Minimally Attended Radar Station.

Almost all the original Cape Romanzof LRRS facilities, including 24 buildings, eight foundations, and antennas, were demolished in 1988. Past activities at Cape Romanzof LRRS, including spills and leaks of petroleum, oils, and lubricants (POL) from tanks or pipes, burial of waste in former landfills, and disposal of small arms ammunition by burning, has resulted in the release of contaminants into the environment. Environmental investigations were initiated in 1989 to determine whether contaminants associated with past installation activities posed an unacceptable level of risk to human health or the environment.

properties.Site_Name: JBER-Ft. Rich SS170P Hangar 4
properties.Problem_Description:
Hangar 4 was built in 1968 on JBER-Richardson. Historically, eleven Tri-Max ™ Compressed Air Foam mobile fire extinguisher units were stored inside on the south side of Hangar 4. No leaks or use of the Tri-Max units were reported; however, due to a gap in facility knowledge, it is possible that a spill or release may have occurred. As a result, a site investigation was conducted in 2022 and four surface soil samples (0 to 2 ft bgs) were collected around Hangar 4. Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) was detected at a concentration of 0.0294 mg/kg in one surface soil sample which prompted further investigations in 2024. 

During the Phase I remedial investigation conducted in 2024 soil and groundwater samples were collected at the site. PFOS was found to exceed DEC's migration to groundwater cleanup levels in surface soil at the site (maximum concentration of 0.085 mg/kg). Groundwater samples did not exceed 18.AAC.75 Table C cleanup levels.

PFAS contamination has not been delineated laterally in any direction or vertically.

properties.Site_Name: JBER-Elmendorf Landfill 6 (LF006)
properties.Problem_Description:
During the 2023 excavation of Taxiway D on JBER-Elmendorf for the JBE054 Runway Extension Project, Landfill 6 (LF006) was partially exposed. Although LF006 was identified during the pre-planning phase of the project as a construction and demolition (C&D) landfill, its location was not accurately recorded, which led to a partial excavation of the landfill. Debris within LF006 was determined to be inconsistent with C&D debris and environmental sampling confirmed the soil within the footprint of LF006 was contaminated with other potential hazardous constituents in addition to perfluoroalkyl or polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). The soil from LF006 was excavated and stockpiled within the PFAS placement area located 250 feet west of the perimeter of the landfill. PFAS-contaminated soil stockpiles are underlain by a 20-mil liner and then covered with a 6-mil to 10-mil liner. 

At the time of site discovery soil was analyzed for mercury, total metals, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), organochlorine pesticides, gasoline range organics (GRO), diesel range organics (DRO), residual range organics (RRO), and per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid, perfluorooctanoic acid, dieldrin, 1-methylnaphthalene, naphthalene, benzo(a)pyrene, benzo(a)anthracene, trichloroethene, and cis-1,2-dichloroethene, exceeded cleanup levels as outlined within 18 AAC 75 Table B1 Method Two – Soil Cleanup Levels Table.

Additionally in the spring of 2025 multiple crushed drums were encountered near the PFAS soil placement area at an approximate depth of 15 feet below ground surface (bgs) while installing a water line. Four 55-gallon steel closed-top drums were identified; the excavation pit was approximately 50 feet long by 30 feet wide. One drum was leaking a small amount of liquid, which appeared to be an oily substance. While there was only a limited volume of liquid available at the time of discovery, two environmental samples were collected and no hazardous substances were identified. 

Following the completion of JBE054 Runway Extension Project a limited field investigation effort will be conducted to further characterize the LF006 landfill and drum site.

properties.Site_Name: Kotzebue Airport - ADF&G Lease Lot
properties.Problem_Description: Four borings were installed for a Phase II investigation. Borings were installed to 11 to 12 ft. The saturated zone started at 5 to 7 ft bgs and permafrost was suspected to start at 7.5 to 8.3 ft bgs.  DRO was found in one sample just above the most stringent cleanup levels. RRO, some VOCs, and PFAS were also observed at concentrations below the cleanup levels.

properties.Site_Name: MSB Station 65 PFAS
properties.Problem_Description: In March 2026, the DEC Drinking Water program received data for properties near the intersection of Palmer-Wasilla Hwy and Seward Meridian Pkwy in Wasilla indicating PFOS and PFOA were present above drinking water action levels in public wells.
